# TO THE MOST SERENE AND ILLUSTRI-
# OUS PRINCE AND LORD,
# FREDERICK THE SECOND, OF DENMARK, NOR-
## way, the Slavs and the Goths King, <note>These were traditional titles used by Danish monarchs; "Slavs" refers to the Wends of the Baltic coast.</note> Duke in
## Schleswig, Holstein, Stormarn, and Dith-
## marschen, Count in Oldenburg and Del-
## menhorst, his

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring intricate foliate and floral scrollwork designs within a square border.</image-desc>

*It is right to believe, Most Serene King, that those ancient Sages and philosophers of old were not moved to the contemplation of Nature and the inquiry into the sources and principles of things in vain. Instead, they were driven by the same impulses that we, in this age, ought rightly to obey, and so they delved into the investigation of causes. For indeed, since mortals were being overwhelmed on all sides by necessities and the hardships of the seasons and weather, and were continually experiencing barrenness <note>In this context, it refers to agricultural failure and famine.</note>, and were being miserably afflicted by new and unusual disturbances of the <term>Elements</term> <note>In the 16th century, the "Elements" (Earth, Air, Fire, Water) were believed to be the building blocks of all physical matter.</note>—earthquakes, floods, and plagues affecting both animals and humans—the more prudent men of higher intellect began to search for a way to meet these calamities with healthy foresight, as Nature is instinctively inclined toward safety and preservation. While they were actively engaged in this inquiry, they discovered that there is a connection of causes: that one thing depends upon another, and that in a wondrous order, later things come from prior ones, lower things from the higher, and weaker things from* <note>original: "à poten-" (likely *à potentioribus*); the text continues "from more powerful ones" on the following page.</note>

<summary>This page is a formal dedication to King Frederick II of Denmark, justifying the study of natural philosophy (science) as a necessary tool for protecting humanity from natural disasters and plagues.</summary>
<keywords>Frederick II of Denmark, natural philosophy, ancient sages, elements, natural disasters, causality, providence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dedication to King Frederick II. It elaborates on the "Great Chain of Being," explaining how the celestial world governs the terrestrial world, and how ancient scholars divided the study of nature into specialized fields like agriculture and husbandry to better predict the seasons.</meta>

—by more powerful things, and that they are preserved, nourished, and governed by them. Consequently, barrenness and fertility, health and disease, and all changes of the lowest things <note>In the Aristotelian worldview, "lowest" or "final" things refer to the material world on Earth, which is subject to change and decay.</note> are derived from the virtues and powers of the prior things <note>The "prior things" are the celestial spheres and stars, believed to be unchanging and perfect.</note>. For these lowest things turned out to be those which life cannot do without, such as **Plants**, **Animals**, **Minerals**, and the blessings of the waters, the lands, the air, and the heavens.

Thus, four sources, nurturers, and guardians immediately became apparent, from whose kind and fertile treasures everything necessary for the use of this life would be supplied. Conversely, from the "silences" <note>A poetic way of describing periods where celestial influence is absent or unfavorable.</note> and hostile dissolutions of these sources, there would occur hopeless harvests, corruptions, plagues, destructions, and infinite disasters. The only task that remained was for men to discern, out of such a great abundance and universality of things, which things agreed with one another; and once this "harmony" was grasped, they had to determine by what laws effects were coupled to their causes.

This was an arduous task, requiring immense observation. Therefore, to manage the difficulty, they divided the work into "provinces" <note>Meaning specialized fields of study or disciplines.</note>. Some men primarily considered the births, transformations, successful yields, failures, and corruptions of grain, vines, trees, herds, bees, and similar things. These men studiously noted the properties of **Animals** and **Plants**—especially domestic ones that provide food and clothing—the nature of seeds, the suitability of various locations, and the associations of the sky and the **stars**, from which the fertile opportunities of the seasons are gathered. Having grasped the causes of fertility, they led a blessed life with a rich confidence in their crops and an undoubting hope for their flocks.

Furthermore, they studiously observed the **decisive stars** <note>original: "Decretoria sydera"; these are specific stars or constellations believed to signal critical moments for planting or harvesting.</note> of the vine, the olive, the crops, and the acorn-bearing trees, as well as the rising and setting of the **stars**—whether auspicious or inauspicious—on account of certain conjunctions of the **Moon** and other **stars** with the prior—

<summary>The author describes how ancient sages identified the celestial causes of earthly fertility and disaster, leading to the birth of specialized sciences like agriculture and meteorology.</summary>

<sig>α 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: runt,</meta>

...joining these observations, they often predicted future barrenness with a great and useful sense of wonder. **Agriculture** was the name given to this **Philosophy**, which was the first and most essential for mortals. Others, in turn, made further progress and, having mastered the human sphere, investigated with tireless effort the natures, properties, preparations, and proper administrations of foods. They also studied the origins, predictions, preventions, and cures of diseases, along with the harmonies between regions, seasons, waters, the air, and the heavens.

This sphere proved to be more obscure and difficult. For the origins of diseases and the governance of natural actions were deeply hidden; neither their "seeds" <term>semina: in early modern science, these were the hidden, fundamental principles or "blueprints" of things</term> nor their locations could be perceived through the senses alone. Therefore, **Physicians**, whose diligence was required in this area, began to pursue deeper contemplations. Drawing closer to the inner sanctuaries of **Nature**, they gradually discovered the skillful workings <term>lithurgias: from the Greek for "service" or "work of the people," here referring to the functional processes of natural forces</term> of invisible seeds by studying the properties of causes and observing their effects.

There was great industry and harmony among mortals in those times. Each person candidly shared their observations with the community. Indeed, they did not believe that the brevity of a single life was sufficient for the **perfection of the Art** <note>original: "Artis absolutio"</note>, which could only emerge from the gathering of such extensive observations. Consequently, disciples—instructed by the observations, laws, and **Methods** of their teachers—added their own findings, confirming the truths of those who came before them, illuminating what was obscure, and expanding what was limited with a vast storehouse of knowledge. But all human endeavors are prone to decay and error. Others could not endure this diligence of the few and the laborious **tedium of Experience**. They sought out methods...

It highlights the importance of multi-generational collaboration and the systematic collection of observations to perfect the "Art" of healing.</summary>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the historical narrative of medicine's decline from a practical, observational science into an abstract, theoretical one. It links the rise of "Hypotheses" and "Geometric Demonstrations" to a period of intellectual laziness, specifically pointing to the influence of medieval Arabic scholars (the "Mauritanians") who favored systematic theory over the difficult, direct observation of Nature.</meta>

...achieved, and Geometric Demonstrations of those things which **Nature** alone can measure. Then, indeed, true **Medicine** gradually began to migrate into the realm of tongues <note>The author suggests that medicine became a matter of rhetoric and debate rather than practical healing.</note>; having abandoned the things themselves and the reliability of observations, they began to seek **Hypotheses** suited to Geometric Demonstrations. 

Thus, the advocacy for heat, cold, moisture, and dryness <note>The four "humors" or qualities of Galenic medicine.</note>, and the administration of **Degrees** <term>graduum: the classification of the intensity of a medicine's qualities on a scale of one to four</term>—described by definite numerical limits—were introduced into Medicine. From these, easy Demonstrations of diseases and remedies could be deduced. **Experience**, however, promised difficulties everywhere. 

Such hypotheses often arose against the natural and legitimate Methods of Medicine; even in the times of **Hippocrates**, they had found Defenders. Yet, rejected by his own diligence and that of his disciples, they immediately collapsed. But twelve hundred years ago, with a repeated incursion, they attacked Medicine, which was then tossed about by various waves. The Age was leaning toward sluggishness and idleness; the cup of dizziness <note>original: "vertiginis"; implying a state of intellectual confusion or intoxication</note> was also being poured out everywhere. 

So, as the labors of **Experience** grew old and the honors of the tongue matured, these theories took deeper roots. Laziness brought aid. For the age embraced the brevity of the Art and the condensed ease proceeding from Hypotheses, rather than the obscure and long exercises of Experience. Now triumph was imminent, with the **Mauritanians** <note>original: "Mauritanis"; referring to the Moorish or Arabic-language physicians of the Middle Ages, whose systematization of Greek medical texts dominated European universities for centuries</note> promising the crown. These men greedily received such fertile and easy Hypotheses. Because the methods for actual practice were sought from these theories in vain, they instead produced certain "experiences"—but they were soft ones, not laborious, not deeply sought, and not unearthed from the inner sanctuaries and treasures of **Nature** by skillful contemplation—

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the critique of theoretical medicine, specifically the transition from empirical observation to rigid, abstract systems. It describes how proponents of "Hypotheses" co-opted the authority of Hippocrates to justify their methods and how the emergence of new, inexplicable diseases eventually forced the medical community to acknowledge "Occult Properties" that their heat-and-cold-based theories could not explain.</meta>

...not rooted out, they added them; and they copiously displayed the spoils of victory in their Treatises and Dispensatories <note>original: "Luminaribus et Dispensatorijs". "Luminaria" refers to foundational "guiding light" texts, while "Dispensatories" were manuals for preparing medicines.</note>. However, although they had adorned these new **Methods** and **Hypotheses** with what seemed to them an unshakeable triumph, **Experience**—the sole parent and nurse of **Medicine**—still seemed to deserve a place in the secret knowledge of both patients and Doctors. This remained true despite the fact that the pedantic precision <term>acribologia: an overly meticulous or hair-splitting way of reasoning or using technical language</term> of Heats and Temperaments <note>The Galenic system of classifying diseases and bodies by degrees of hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> promised riches that would last forever.

Consequently, they placed **Hippocrates** at the head of their own ignorance. They unjustly boasted of his **Experiences**, and by foreign and forced interpretations, they compelled those divine Oracles <note>Likely referring to the *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates, which were treated with the authority of holy scripture.</note> to comply with their theories—oracles which the old man himself had actually submitted to the judgment of **Experience**. Thus, whenever the battle line had to be drawn against the **Empirics** <note>Physicians who relied on observation and trial-and-error rather than overarching theories.</note>, they would bring forward **Hippocrates** (whom they also admired) even against his will, making him a witness to their injustice and—if the fates allow—perhaps one day their punisher. 

This **Monarchy** reigned far and wide, and it maintained its unconquered empire up to our own Century. Everyone flocked to it—Greeks, Arabs, Italians, Germans, and French—and they signed their names to such a powerful Monarchy, bound by a pledge of perpetual servitude. 

New diseases were arising, and still arise daily, which do not respond to **Hypotheses** based on heat and cold. Treatments for these diseases, established in vain through remedies found by the service of these theoretical **Methods**, fail. In these cases, wondrous subtleties were sought, and all the "Mysteries" of Heat and Dryness were produced. When these theories fell silent and stood stunned at the wonder of this unexpected innovation <note>The author refers to the appearance of new, complex diseases that the old four-humor system could not explain.</note>, **Occult Properties** <term>Occultae proprietates: hidden qualities or powers in substances that act in ways not explained by the traditional four elements (hot, cold, wet, dry)</term> secretly crept in. The **Hippocratic Powers** rejoiced that their neglected desires had once again found favor with Mortals.

<summary>The author argues that medical theorists hijacked Hippocrates’ legacy to support abstract systems, but these theories eventually failed when faced with new diseases that required acknowledging "occult properties" beyond simple humors.</summary>
<keywords>Hippocrates, Experience vs Theory, Galenic Medicine, Medical History, Occult Properties, Empirics, Scholasticism</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page, where the author describes how established physicians were forced to reckon with "Occult Properties" when their traditional theories of "Heats and Temperaments" failed. The catchword "De" at the bottom of the previous page would have led into a discussion about these hidden powers.</meta>

But these **Properties** <term>Proprietates: the specific, hidden powers of a substance that do not come from its temperature or moisture, such as the ability of a magnet to pull iron</term> lay hidden and concealed, and no path lay open to reach their vital domains. And if anyone, compelled by the necessity of diseases or out of pity for the complaints of the sick, had more eagerly begun investigations into these **Properties**, he—promptly mindful of the trust placed in him—either assigned the powers of the **Properties** an obscure name at least, or subjected them to the governance of the **Qualities** <note>The four "Manifest Qualities" of Galenic medicine: Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry.</note>.

However, those who were mindful of liberty and devotion, and who attempted to uncover the obscurities of the **Properties** through the difficulties of **Experience**, the persistence of labor, and frequent meditation, and sought to demonstrate easier ways of access, were called **Deserters**, **Empirics**, and **Mountebanks** <note>original: "Circumforanei" — literally "those who hang around the marketplace." It was a derogatory term for itinerant healers or quacks who did not have formal university training.</note>. Their efforts were also met with disapproval because they seemed to demand the labor and sweat of Physicians. Because of these difficulties, their schools and assemblies soon lost their students.

Meanwhile, diseases multiply, and the old ones appear "illegitimate," no longer matching the descriptions written by our Ancestors <note>The author is likely referring to the emergence of "new" diseases in the 16th century, like syphilis or the English Sweat, which did not fit ancient Greek or Roman medical texts.</note>. Physicians marvel at the difficulty and the weakness of their remedies; they flee to **Experience**, even if unwillingly. They eagerly accept medicinal woods <note>original: "ligna." Likely referring to exotic woods like *Guaiacum* (Holy Wood) imported from the Americas to treat syphilis.</note> from merchants and ointments from **Mountebanks** for the cure of many diseases; they compose remedies from both the **Manifest** and the **Occult**.

It would be fitting, above all, to recall the memory of human liberty and to weigh the necessities of our present calamities. Then, we should approach the contemplation of **Nature**, **Causes**, and **Properties**, and not be deterred from such a fruitful province by any difficulties, expenses, or labors. We are bound by no sense of shame to the Greeks or the Arabs <note>Referring to the authority of Galen (Greek) and Avicenna (Arabic), whose systems dominated European medicine for centuries.</note>. We are the servants of the sick, for whom the **Most High** <note>original: "Altissimus" — referring to God.</note> created **Medicine**, and having created it, committed it to our diligent labor.

<summary>The author critiques the medical establishment for ignoring "Occult Properties" in favor of easy, outdated theories, and argues that the rise of new, incurable diseases proves that physicians must look beyond ancient Greek and Arab authorities toward hands-on experience and nature.</summary>
<keywords>Medical Reform, Occult Properties, Empiricism, Galenic Qualities, Mountebanks, New Diseases, Medical Liberty, Experience vs Theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author’s dedication to the King. Following the previous discussion on how traditional medicine failed to account for "hidden properties," the author now describes his personal journey into the controversial world of Paracelsian medicine and his attempts to reconcile these "new" ideas with ancient wisdom.</meta>

Concerning these matters and plans, I have often reflected, **Most Serene King**, as one who has devoted myself since early youth to **Medical** and **Philosophical** studies. But because in the works of the **Art** <note>Meaning the "Medical Art" or the profession of medicine.</note>, I have often discovered that **Galenic Theorems** <note>The traditional medical theories based on the work of Galen, a 2nd-century Greek physician.</note> (and even less so their **Remedies**) cannot suffice in the treatment of the most difficult diseases, and hearing everywhere throughout **Germany** certain **Paracelsian Medicines** being championed: I began to read through his writings more diligently. In these, a **Charybdis** <note>A dangerous mythological whirlpool; the author uses it here to describe a dizzying sea of intellectual confusion.</note> of difficulties was presented, caused by the obscure novelty of the names, the multitude of apparent contradictions, the riddle of the **Preparations**, and a new way of philosophizing. 

But certainly, the greater the obscurity appeared, the more my desire and diligence grew. Therefore, with persistence, sleepless nights, tireless study, labors, travels, expenses, and dangers, I strove to overcome the difficulties placed in my way; and through the faithful practice of the **Preparations**, I gradually learned the natures, the "dwellings" <note>original: "diversoria" — referring to the specific places within a substance where its medicinal power resides.</note>, and the compositions of the **Properties**. 

Then, turning my attention vigorously to the contemplation of **Generations** and **Transplantations** <note>In this context, "Transplantation" refers to the Paracelsian idea of moving a disease or a vital force from one body or substance to another.</note>, I began to unfold the decrees of the **Ancients**—who had described the history of **Nature**, the properties of the **Elements** and seeds, the cultivation of fields, observations of the stars, and the **Generations** of **Plants**, **Minerals**, and **Animals**—with the greatest benefit. For these explained the logic of the orders, the variety of interpretations, and the methods of vital **Astrology** <term>Astrology: in Paracelsian medicine, this does not mean predicting the future, but rather understanding how celestial forces and "firmaments" influence the health and growth of earthly things.</term> which **PARACELSUS** uses in all his **Philosophy** and **Medicine**. <meta>This page continues the author's narrative of his intellectual journey. Having previously mentioned his study of Paracelsus and the "dwellings" of natural properties, he now explains his decision to synthesize ancient and modern philosophies into a unified system to find a universal cure.</meta>

...strengthened also by the authority of the Philosophers, whose names it is not necessary to list here, I decided to establish a critical evaluation <note>original: "censura" — here meaning a scholarly examination or critique</note> of both Philosophies <note>Referring to the "Ancient" Galenic/Aristotelian tradition and the "New" Paracelsian/Chemical tradition.</note>. Relying upon philosophical freedom, I first established the immovable foundations of **Nature**, from which I have derived the causes of effects that are subject to **Nature's** command, the principles of actions, **Mechanical** processes, and orderly explanations of causes. It was pleasing then to have overcome the shadows of things; more pleasing to have discovered the **Harmony** of the ancient Philosophers; but most pleasing indeed to have understood the kind providence of **Nature**—that she has destined such a mild and friendly **Balsam** <note>In this context, "Balsam" refers to a vital healing essence or life-force believed to reside within all living things, a key concept in 17th-century vitalist medicine.</note> for the cure of all diseases, by whose protection the harsh ailments of Mortals are kindly revived.

Nor did I decide to keep this evaluation for myself alone. My mind recoils from the crime of **Envy**. It is right to imitate the simplicity of our ancestors and the harmony of their studies, and to assist present needs through a fellowship of duties. Therefore, whatever I have gained through labors, sleepless nights, studies, and travels that can illuminate **Medicine** and **Philosophy**, I have, as far as possible, honestly shared with others—and I will share more, if I perceive that this "offspring" <note>A common metaphorical way for authors of this period to refer to their published books.</note> has not come into the light in vain.

It was certainly an arduous task here to give light to the obscure, grace to the despised, novelty to the old, credibility to the doubtful, and names to the unknown. And I have earned forgiveness in this way too: that I have often attempted unusual paths of interpretation. For, following in the footsteps of the Philosophers, I have joined <note>The Latin text ends on a partial word "ad-", completed by the catchword "iunxi," forming "adiunxi" (I joined/added).</note> many things omitted by others...

<meta>This page continues the author's dedication to his royal patron. Having established a harmony between Ancient and Modern philosophies on the previous page, he now describes his synthesis of these traditions as a "living" philosophy, contrasted against the "dead" materialistic views of his contemporaries.</meta>

I joined them, expanded the narrowness of their Methods, and made the scattered families of things work in harmony. I have been neither a mere reciter of others' words, nor a bare transcriber of texts. From the very same fountains from which the Ancients and the more recent interpreters of hidden **Nature** drew, I have channeled my own streams. Often, while looking upon the confluence of these streams, I mitigated the weariness of my nightly labors <term>lucubrations</term> <note>original: "lucubrationum" — scholarly work performed by candlelight at night</note> with joyful recreation.

Truly, to your Highness, most Serene King <note>original: "Rex Serenissime"</note>, I wished to dedicate these labors of mine, so that I might declare the veneration of a modest mind with at least some proof, and celebrate the favor and benevolence of your Highness with a grateful sign of my goodwill. Kings, and even Monarchs, once kindly received such offspring <note>original: "foetus" — figuratively used here for the intellectual "fruits" or "products" of his mind</note> into their protection. They themselves also strenuously sought the mysteries of **Nature**, to the great benefit of Mortals. For these things are vital, and they employ the services of living spirits <note>In 17th-century science, "vital spirits" were thought to be the subtle substances that animated the body and linked the soul to the flesh.</note>.

Our current age has fallen away toward a purely corporeal **Philosophy** <note>original: "corpoream Philosophiam" — the author is likely criticizing a growing trend toward mechanical materialism that views the world as "dead" matter without a spiritual or vital spark</note>, and follows after the dead shadows of things, in which there is nothing worthy of Kings, nor useful to others. But if I perceive that these first efforts <note>original: "rudimenta"</note> of my nightly labors have pleased your Highness, I can promise greater and more elaborate works, which will satisfy the wishes of many. He who moderates the hearts of Kings, who alone can bring about happy governments, who grants the **Wisdom** through which Kings reign—God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Deus Opt. Max." — a standard abbreviation for Deus Optimus Maximus</note>—may He keep your Highness surviving and flourishing for as long as possible...

Galen attempted to bring this vast sea of Medicine and such great confusion among Physicians back into order. He did so after discovering that his teachers had handed down the art through mere persuasions and probable conjectures. Not content with a vague and shifting heap of hypotheses—from which opinions and deceptive operations arise, rather than Science and effective methods of action—he long sought certain laws of Demonstration <term>Demonstration: in a classical sense, a logical proof that leads to certain knowledge, like those in geometry</term> with tireless study, care, and travels. 

Finally, by entering the schools of the Geometers <note>mathematicians who followed the rigorous logical methods of Euclid</note>, he discovered the most exquisite Demonstrations. Having quickly acquired a wealth and mastery of these, he adapted them with great ease to medical theorems. Therefore, in the manner of the Geometers, he established the Principles and Axioms <term>Axioms: self-evident truths that serve as the foundation for a system of belief or science</term> of his art: that all things arise from the four Elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>; that the Elements are mixed by certain weights and measures; that a balance <note>original: "symmetriam"</note> of the Mixture is the producer of health, while an imbalance <note>original: "ametriam"</note> produces disease and death; that the actions and virtues of all things come forth from the Elements; and that the specific Form, or essential property of each thing, [derives] from a certain Ele[ment]...

# WHAT MEDICINE IS, AND WHAT
# FOUNDATIONS IT HAS
->in Nature.<-

## CHAPTER II.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'Q' decorated with intricate floral patterns and foliage.</image-desc>
Those who have written about medical matters until now have said that Medicine is an art for preserving the health of the human body and driving away diseases, properly administering all things. We, however, do not seek those common definitions. What we are considering is something greater: whether there is some subject in Nature—a substance accessible to the senses—which, when properly prepared and administered, can remove human ailments. If so, it could truly be called "Medicine," and the legitimate management of its internal processes <note>original: *oeconomiae*. In this context, "economy" refers to the organized functional systems and "housekeeping" of the body.</note> could be distinguished by the title of an "art," and its director justly called an "artist" <note>original: *artificem*. This refers to a skilled practitioner or craftsman who works in harmony with natural laws, likely reflecting the author's Hermetic or Paracelsian leanings.</note>. For in this way, all mechanical arts receive their material from Nature. They exquisitely investigate its nature, properties, and all its conditions, searching with great effort to find by what preparation, by what means, and by what mechanical process it can best be adapted to human uses and needs. Once these things are discovered and understood, they establish an "art" and produce "artists." Yet there is a very great range among these arts. For some deal with subjects...

<meta>catchword: mate-</meta>

The author argues that medicine should be defined by how the physician (the "artist") prepares and manages natural substances to heal the body.</summary>

...dominate the materials, and clothe them in figures and forms conceived in the mind, according to their own will: such as **sculptors**, **smiths**, **potters**, and so on. Others, because they handle more hidden materials that are not so manifest to the senses, assign the greater part of the work to Nature; they serve as attendants, applying what is necessary and granting all the business and care to Nature: such as the **cultivation of fields** <note>original: *agris cultura*. Referring to agriculture.</note>. Some hold a middle way, performing their business through the benefit of both Art and Nature: such as **glassmakers**, **goldsmiths**, and those who **separate metals and minerals**.

Hippocrates certainly placed Medicine among those arts which grant the governance and command to Nature. For he used to say that **Natures are the healers of diseases**, while the **Physician is the servant** <note>original: *Naturas morborum medicatrices, Medicum uerò ministrum*. This is a central tenet of Hippocratic medicine, often phrased as *Vis Medicatrix Naturae*, suggesting the body has an innate ability to heal itself.</note>. Others have dared to assign equal dignity to the Physician, and sometimes even a higher status; but they do not notice that Hippocrates—speaking with a very loose and ambiguous definition of Medicine—was referring to diseases produced from the elements and from an internal seed <note>original: *semine*. In this context, "seed" likely refers to the internal, generative principle or essence from which a disease grows, a concept central to Paracelsian philosophy.</note>.

And we, when we speak of Medicine here, do not mean **bloodletting** <note>original: *uenam secare*. Literally "to cut a vein," the most common medical procedure of the era.</note>, **resetting dislocated limbs**, **amputating dead parts**, or **curing those with hernias and stones by cutting** <note>original: *hernicosos & calculosos sectione sanare*. These conditions were traditionally treated by specialized surgeons or "lithotomists" rather than academic physicians.</note>; instead, we mean the removal of those radical diseases, born in the body from a "seed," by using vital and powerful remedies. We shall speak of **surgical administrations**, the proper **diet** for the sick, **exercises**, and similar matters once we have introduced those things which are essential for the Physician.

Many will wonder at this point that we, in a matter so easy... <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "ras" suggests the next word is "horas" (hours/time).</note>

*   For **altered qualities**, he used hot, cold, moist, or dry; 
*   For **faults in the causes**, he used purges, smoothing agents, thinning agents, cutting agents, relaxants, astringents, and concocting agents.

He <note>Referring to Galen, mentioned on the previous page.</note> is found to have noted that dissimilar substances, often marked by contrary properties, are contained within a single and simple thing—though he touched upon this matter only very lightly, as if in jest. And because certain powers within "simple" remedies <note>A "simple" is a medicinal herb used on its own, rather than as part of a complex mixture.</note> often—nearly always—opposed the physician's intended goals (whether due to an immoderate power of action, or an unusual and unpleasant taste or smell, or because the plant's powers worked in an opposite direction), he removed all such obstacles through mixing and composition. Whatever was lacking, he added. 

The **Arabs** <note>original: *Arabes*. This refers to the influential medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna or Rhazes, whose works dominated European medicine for centuries.</note>, using an abundance of sugar and honey, transformed the universal bitterness of remedies into a wonderful sweetness. They also introduced new "corrections" <note>In historical pharmacy, a "correction" was an ingredient added to a medicine to mitigate its toxic or violent side effects.</note> for violent medicaments: preparing **scammony** with **quinces**, **colocynth** <note>Also known as "bitter apple," a powerful laxative.</note> with milk, and **hellebore** with radish root. 

And yet, perceiving the violence of the symptoms and the sinking of the patient's strength (however much they believed they had removed the poison through their "corrections"), they found it a great necessity to add **Strengthening remedies** and **Heart-tonics** <note>original: *Confortatiua & Cordialia*. These were medicines intended to bolster the "vital spirits" or the heart during aggressive treatment.</note>. They filled every place with a medley of these things, proud of their apothecary jars as if in a victory triumph. They believed—as was indeed the case—that the final result was the only way to judge the completion and perfection of their work. 

I notice that no other way of healing has been accepted until now in the schools or in the courts of Princes. ...liberated [the vital principle] from qualities, asserting that it is clothed neither in heat, nor cold, nor moisture, nor dryness, nor any such Aristotelian qualities <note>The four primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—which Aristotle believed were the building blocks of all physical matter</note>, going beyond all of Galen's <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the influential Greek physician whose theories of the four humors dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> expectations. Therefore, he named the entire substance the **substantial form** <term>substantial form: a philosophical term for the essential nature or "soul" of a thing that gives it its specific identity and properties</term>.

Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity</note>, having considered the differences between the natural causes from which actions flow, discovered that some causes—both in the development of diseases and in their cure—are sluggish, weak, and lack a fixed or vital impression. # IDEA MEDICINAE
# [The Ideal of Medicine]

[The Medical Art] diligently investigates the bases and foundations of human Nature. The rising and setting of the stars, the periods of the **Planets**, defined by certain intervals of time, their conjunctions, oppositions, impressions, and the effects which they print upon the **inferior Elements** <note>In the worldview of the time, the "inferior elements" refer to the terrestrial realm (earth, water, air, fire) which was believed to be governed and influenced by the "superior" celestial bodies.</note>: the origins of comets, of winds, thunder, lightning, rain, dew, frost, and so on; the tides of the **Ocean** and their ebb and flow, the diversities of Lands; the distinctions of **Plants**, the origins, progressions, and separations of **Metals** and **Minerals**, the natures of **Animals**, and their modes of reproduction—these are investigated by the sleepless labors of many **Philosophers**. 

While each individual takes for himself a small portion from this vastness of things to be examined separately, believing that the lifespan and talent of one man is by no means sufficient to comprehend the arrangement of such a vast Province, the **Physician**, with untiring study, alone scrutinizes the universal **Economy** <note>original: "Oeconomiam"; referring to the organized system, divine management, or internal "housekeeping" of the natural world.</note> of all Nature. He examines the decrees of **Astronomers** and **Astrologers**; he collects the reasonings of **Meteorologists**, **Physicists**, and **Herbalists**. He consults the masters of **Agriculture** and those skilled in **Metallic** matters, learning their experiences and observations. He diligently investigates the natures of **Animals**; and he encompasses all these things within Principles, Elements, and certain laws of **Generations** and <term>Transplantations <note>The concept of "Transplantation" in this context refers to the movement of life-force, properties, or disease-principles between different natural bodies, such as from a plant to a human or from one metal to another.</note></term>. Having perceived these things, he descends to the **human Commonwealth** <note>original: "humanam Rempublicam"; a metaphor for the human body as a complex, governed society of parts.</note>, and by a certain divine **Analogy**, [he relates] the arrangement of the **greater World** <note>The Macrocosm, or the universe at large, which was believed to be mirrored perfectly within the human "Microcosm."</note>

He <note>Hippocrates</note> would have rejected the names of **Hot**, **Cold**, **Moist**, and **Dry** a thousand times if he had foreseen the errors, follies, and ruins that were later introduced into the medical profession on their account. With a suspicious ease, they also constructed the laws of cures based on the harmony and opposition of these qualities. They argued that those highest and most intense qualities can only be found in the "highest bodies" <note>the primary celestial or elemental spheres</note>; and that these are not infinite, but only four in number, where they noted the heat of fire (though they strongly doubt both). 

They would have acted more rightly if they had derived the orders of the Elements from the diversity and number of **procreations** <note>original: "procreationum"; the act of generating or bringing forth new life and substances</note>. For in each individual Element, there are notable differences in procreations and **seeds** <note>term: "seeds" (semina); in this context, the internal formative power that determines what a substance will become</note>; although neighbor agrees greatly with neighbor, which results in them forming a single globe. Each **Element**, therefore, is abundantly sufficient for producing and preserving its own fruits; it is not destitute, needing to borrow particles from elsewhere. 

Nor do we abolish the harmony and consensus of the Elements. They are gathered together through the benefit of the **Seeds**. The **Stars** <note>original: "Astra"</note> are the bonds of all things. From them depend the strifes, friendships, progressions, proportions, penetrations, impressions, and the governing of the entire **Creation**. 

The Elements are guardians, nurses, and wombs <note>original: "matrices"; a central concept in Paracelsian philosophy where each element acts as a mother-environment for specific life forms</note>. Here, as if in an abyss, the **seeds** <note>original: "semina"</note> lie hidden, destined to come forth at their appointed times. When they have completed their task within the restless cycle of movements, they return to their lodgings with a great longing for rest, leading a happier life there than when they were confined here by time and place. For since seeds are nearly innumerable—serving particular duties and the unfolding of Nature—if they are to be united, they require a more communal and thus more powerful life. We find this preserved with marvelous craftsmanship in all the works of Nature. 

Confirmed now by these and similar properties, I say: **THE ELEMENTS ARE PLACES, WOMBS, AND DWELLINGS, FORTIFIED WITH A VITAL AND POWERFUL FORCE, WHICH NOURISH THE SEEDS CONSECRATED FOR GENERATION AT THEIR APPOINTED TIMES.**

### PHILOSOPHICAL STUDIES

[They] awaken [life], lead it toward **maturity**, and grant a **refuge** to those who have finished their service, blessed in unchanging rest. And because they are places, necessity demands that they be **incorporeal** <note>original: "incorporea"; meaning the Elements act as the space or "container" rather than the physical "stuff" itself</note>. For unless they were free from the laws of **dimension**, they could never so easily contain such a vast multitude of bodies, principles, and seeds. Yet they are not infinite, as a **vital power** <note>original: "vitali virtute"</note> prescribes their ends and boundaries. Within these limits not only must the Elements themselves remain, but also the seeds, the principles, and even the bodies, however much they may triumph in the proud display of their physical dimensions. They are empty or void by a similar providence: otherwise, by showing unequal favor and being more bound to certain seeds, they would have received the natures of others more obscurely and presented them as anything but pure.

And this is the legitimate concept of the **Elements**, derived from their properties and duties. If we follow this path, we shall maintain that the Elements are neither mixed, nor corruptible, nor fleeting. By analogy and the similarity of their properties—and confirmed by the authority of the **Philosophers**—we have applied the name of "Elements" to other things as well, both here and in many other places. It is fitting for our concepts of things to imitate the stability of their true essences; **names**, after all, are subject to the discretion of the craftsmen <note>The author suggests that while the "essence" of a thing is fixed by nature, the "names" we use are tools chosen by scholars and practitioners</note>.

Whoever has contemplated the Principles more deeply than the laws of Generations and Transplantations <note>original: *Transplantationum*; in this context, the process of moving vital forces or qualities between different organisms or states of being</note> require, their decrees we neither reject nor approve in this place: for they dispute about Principles in another way, and the meaning of the word is broad. For proper Principles are joined to each individual order of things. When **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a pioneer of the medical revolution of the Renaissance</note> says that all bodies consist of **Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury** <note>Known as the *Tria Prima*, these were Paracelsus's three fundamental substances of all matter, representing stability (Salt), inflammability (Sulfur), and volatility (Mercury)</note>, he does not contradict **Aristotle**, who established the Principles of things as **Matter, Form, and Privation** <note>The three components of Aristotle’s theory of change: the underlying stuff (Matter), its specific nature (Form), and the absence of a form it is meant to have (Privation)</note>; nor **Plato**, who says that **God, the Exemplar <note>The "Idea" or divine blueprint</note>, and Matter** are the Principles of all things. Indeed, each of them scrutinizes the different economies <term>Oeconomia; the internal management and functional balance of a living system</term> of creatures. To us, the purpose is to declare the causes and processes of Generations and Transplantations.

Thus, we have demonstrated the properties of the Elements and the seeds. Yet, we have also perceived that something is still lacking before they can fulfill the public services <note>original: *lithurgias*; here used to mean the functional roles or duties performed by natural forces</note> of Generations and Transplantations <note>original: *Transplantationum*; the process of moving vital forces or qualities between different states of being</note> from their own hidden depths upon this worldly stage. It was necessary, therefore, to add a nature of such a kind that, through its divisible quality, it would allow for the necessary unfolding <note>original: *explicationes*; the physical manifestation or "unrolling" of hidden potential into the visible world</note> of times, places, and all dimensions. This nature would set a limit to the vital powers of the seeds and thus close the doors of universal Nature. This is the nature of bodies. 

Although, to the unthinking judgment of our senses, bodies seem to be easily explained and free from obscurity, nevertheless, when we investigate their origin, differences, and conditions, many things arise that have exhausted the minds of many philosophers. Bold and reckless mortality promises itself knowledge of invisible things through the service of the senses, even though visible and physical things cannot be fully grasped by the laws of those same senses. 

Certain external traces of bodies have been grasped—such as proportions, weights, colors, heat and cold, smells, tastes, sizes, shapes, and numbers—yet these things are merely external additions <note>original: *adventitia*; qualities that are added to a substance from the outside rather than being part of its essential nature</note> to the bodies themselves. By means of these faculties, and through the fertile sketching of Methods <note>The formal systems of logic and science used during the Renaissance to categorize knowledge</note>, we attempt with impious recklessness to interpret invisible and even heavenly things; nor does the ill-fated audacity of the Giants <note>A reference to the mythological Giants who attempted to storm heaven and were struck down by the gods; a warning against intellectual pride</note> deter us. But if we first investigate the origin of both the bodies themselves and the qualities inherent within those bodies—

They begin to demonstrate differences that are manifest to reason—and, in the lowest orders of things, even to the senses. Therefore, the **Elements** and the <term>Seeds</term> <note>original: *Semina*; the spiritual blueprints or vital forces that direct the growth of all living things</note>, which we have just discussed, were once unified in their original sources. But after they were commanded by the immutable decree of eternal law to administer the <term>economy</term> <note>original: *œconomia*; the divine management or ordered arrangement</note> of the worldly age, they were separated into distinct duties, existences, lives, and essences. Nor should we imagine that these highly ordered things emerged from confusion, or from **Chaos**; rather, they came from the eternal treasures of divine wisdom.

In this primary constitution of **Creatures**, it was necessary for the seeds—having set out from their source—to be established in another foundation. Nor was it right for them to remain at rest here; instead, through the constant multiplication of fruits, they were to govern the successions of **Generations** and **Transplantations**, and so complete the defined periods of the world's <term>Revolution</term> <note>original: *Reuolutio*; the cyclical unfolding of time or cosmic stages</note>. If it was necessary for the <term>images</term> <note>original: *imagines*; the formal patterns or reflections of the divine blueprints</note> of seeds to travel abroad, it was also right for a Nature consistent with those images to accompany the **Elements**. The first difference among bodies is derived from the orders of the Elements: namely, that some are earthy, others watery, others airy, and others celestial. These differ greatly in their ability to penetrate, their mobility, and their power of action. 

Furthermore, some bodies are more significantly marked by the properties of the Elements, while others are marked by the properties of the seeds. Those more marked by the properties of the Elements are those in which no internal <term>dynamis</term> <note>original: *dynamis*; a Greek term meaning power, potency, or vital force—the "engine" of a living thing</note> lies hidden—at least, only sterile qualities such as heat, cold, moisture, dryness, lightness, and heaviness, in which there is no **fertile impression** <note>original: *impressio fœcunda*; a creative or formative "stamp" left by nature that allows a thing to grow or produce fruit</note>; they are even found to be plainly tasteless and without flavor. 

Bodies of this kind have been called "Elements" by many Philosophers until now; and yet they are actually the fruits of seeds and other Elements, serving the process of generation through a perennial flow and irrigation. Such is the nature of our earth, water, air, and fire; such is the nature of very many celestial impressions, such as snow, rain, certain winds, heat, cold, dryness, moisture, and similar atmospheric impressions. Almost all springs and rivers are contained within this classification.

In the end, these "veils of ignorance" were so pleasing to them that they even used those names as titles for their books—books that will stand as future witnesses to their errors and lack of skill. ### PHILOSOPHICAL [MATTERS]

...through a higher **Analysis** <note>original: "Analysi" — here referring to chemical resolution or "spagyric" breaking down of matter into its parts.</note>, they investigated the **Principles** of natural things. Not content only with the testimony of the senses, they added the skillful resolution of bodies. By the benefit of this process, once the separation of substances from which individual bodies were composed was performed, those properties that were previously hidden by the power of the mixture came into view. Then, at last, it became clear by which Principles so many and such varied effects were produced. Thus, from the vast province of species, distinct and separate Individuals clearly demonstrated the nearest sources of actions.

For a long time, there was much doubt regarding **Opium**, specifically by what reason its power of stupefying <note>original: "stupefaciendi" — the power to numb or induce sleep.</note> excelled despite such great bitterness. We, having performed a separation of its substances, discovered a **sulfur** or oily substance that is plainly **narcotic** <note>original: "narcoticum" — a sleep-inducing or numbing agent.</note>. We had previously seen sulfurs of the same nature, by the same diligent labor, in many parts of Nature: in <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "uitriolo" — a historical term for various metal sulfates, often associated with acidity and medicinal potency.</note>, <term>nitre</term> <note>original: "nitro" — potassium nitrate or saltpeter.</note>, in almost all salts, in common sulfur, and in very many herbs. 

Therefore, we ascribed this property of opium neither to heat, nor to cold, nor to humidity, nor to dryness, nor to thinness, nor to thickness <note>The author is listing the "four primary qualities" used by Galenic physicians to explain medicine.</note>, but to such a specific body—that is, to a **narcotic sulfur**. By the same separation, anatomy, and analysis, we discovered in opium a certain **diaphoretic salt** <note>original: "sal quoddam diaphoreticum" — a salt that induces sweating.</note>, which moves sweats by penetrating through a subtle resolution. We can similarly demonstrate its likeness in many other parts of Nature. To the bodies discovered in this kind of separation, we have given the names **Salt**, **Sulfur**, and **Mercury**.

...expressed. If one thing is named, he understands unity; if many, he brings forth a multitude: if he names two, or three, or four, etc., he suddenly releases just as many <term>Syrians or Parmenos</term> <note>These are stock characters from ancient Greek "New Comedy." The author uses them as a metaphor for a sudden crowd or a variety of distinct individuals emerging from a single source.</note>. If it is called "Elemental," it contains the **Elements** within itself; if "seminal," it contains the **seeds**; if "corporeal," **bodies**; if "spiritual," **spirits**, and so on.

Therefore, when Hippocrates says that all things consist of **Fire** and **Water**, he does not contradict himself—even though in his book *On Human Nature*, he declared that the bodies of all things are constituted from the **hot**, the **cold**, the **moist**, and the **dry**. Nor does he contradict Thales, who declared that all things consist of **Water**; nor others who seem to derive the origins of things from **Water** and **Earth**. Whatever names the Philosophers have used, they intend for the powers of the other elements to be present, as they are required to complete the process of <term>Generation</term> <note>The biological process of coming into being or procreation.</note>.

Thus, in the book *On Human Nature*, he says man consists of the hot, the cold, the moist, and the dry, or of **Blood**, **Phlegm**, and **both types of Bile** <note>Yellow and Black Bile; these are the "Four Humors" of classical medicine, believed to regulate health and temperament.</note>. Nor for that reason did he neglect the conditions of the **Seeds**, nor did he propose Elements that were empty or deprived of seeds; rather, having established the Elements everywhere as a defined root and matter, he adds the "separations" and the "progressions" of the seeds.

And since he admits that "nothing new is made" in <term>Generation</term>, he certainly understands that the seeds had previously lain hidden in the Elements, however they were positioned or named. This is the occasion for all errors: when he says that human bodies consist of the hot, the cold, the moist, and the dry, many understand these as absolute Elements,

...the danger of flight from the **Mechanical Spirits** <note>original: *Spiritibus Mechanicis*; the active, operational forces that carry out the "work" of nature</note> and the **Principles of Generations**, and in this way we have removed that fear. Rather, it happens because, at the very beginnings of **Generations**, the spirits have formed the rudiments of bodies that are still thin and weak. These fragile beginnings are exposed to the flowing influences and impressions of other **Stars**, and they are often deprived of the kind nurturing of their locations. In this <term>liturgy</term> <note>original: *lithurgia*; the author views the processes of nature as a sacred "service" or ritual work</note>, if all circumstances are opposed to the **Generation**, the physical bodies will be the first to flee and will hasten toward destruction; yet the spirits and the Principles will persist unmovably within their own Abysses and Roots. 

If, however, the astral impressions are more moderate and the locations are not entirely hostile, **Nature**—having abandoned the hope of a perfect generation—will attempt a plan of **Transplantation**. In such a case, "that which she does not wish" will happen, to speak with **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician; the author refers to the idea that nature adapts to circumstances, sometimes producing an alternative result when the primary one is blocked</note>. Having set aside the severity of her own laws, she will broker a peace, conceding equal—and sometimes even superior—roles in the administration of her Province to another force. 

All these things will soon appear more clearly through examples. For now, let it suffice to have shown that bodies are contained and sustained by spirits, and these spirits are in turn sustained by **Principles** or **seminal reasons** <note>original: *seminariis Rationibus*; a concept from Stoic philosophy referring to the invisible, rational blueprints or "forming powers" that dictate how a seed grows</note>.

There are even plants that do not wish to "travel" <note>meaning they cannot be easily transplanted to different climates or soils</note>, as Hippocrates says of **Sylphium** <note>A medicinal plant highly prized in antiquity, famously difficult to cultivate outside its native Cyrene; it is now believed to be extinct.</note>. Thus the vine loves the hills; the willow, poplar, **loosestrife** <note>original: *lysimachia*</note>, and **smartweed** <note>original: *persicaria*</note> love the waters; clover, **satyrion** <note>a type of orchid historically associated with aphrodisiac qualities</note>, and the **cowslip** <note>original: *herba Paralysis*; literally "the palsy herb," named for its use in treating tremors or paralysis</note> love the meadows; thyme, oregano, **ground-pine** <note>original: *chamepytis*</note>, and **poly-mountain** <note>original: *polium*</note> love the mountains, and so on.

# THE IDEA OF MEDICINE

Thus, the **Southern winds** are described by **Hippocrates** <note>The famous ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC), often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> as "making one hard of hearing, sluggish, heavy-headed, and debilitating" <note>original Greek: βαρύηκοι, νωθροὶ, καρυβαρικοὶ, διαλυτικοὶ</note>, not because they are merely moist and hot, but because their "bodies" are equipped with the properties of **Opiates, Hemlocks, Nightshades**, and so on. Their physical forms are dissimilar, but the harmony of their actions and properties creates a likeness in the eyes of Philosophers.

Again, he adds the properties of the **North Wind**: "But if it is the North wind, there are coughs, throat irritations, hard bowels, painful urination, shivering, and pains of the sides and chests" <note>original Greek: ἦν δὲ βόρειον ἦ βῆχες, φάρυγγες, κοιλίαι σκληραὶ, δυσουρίαι φρικώδεες ὀδύναι πλευρέων στηθέων</note>. First, they reduced Nature into narrow straits by proposing only bodies and those famous **Qualities**: Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness. Having laid these foundations with idle and limitless doubts, they began to investigate: whether bodies (that is, the "Substances of the Elements," as they interpret them) or the **Qualities** (heat, moisture, cold, dryness) were mixed entirely, part-for-part.

Certainly, they argued about many things more childishly than those who never claimed the title of "Philosopher" for themselves. 

But if an account must be given for every idle word <note>A reference to the biblical warning in Matthew 12:36 that people will be judged for every careless word spoken.</note>, what a great debt will remain for those who wrongly spend their lives on these "usuries" of time? We find many such questions throughout their entire system of Philosophy and Medicine.

...explained the logic in this way: that those four simple **Natures of the World** <term>Mundi Naturas: A term for the fundamental building blocks of the universe, here synonymous with the four Elements.</term>—that is, the **Elements**—converge with somewhat equal forces. As for the **Qualities** <term>Qualitates: Specifically the "Primary Qualities": Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness.</term>, they are mixed entirely throughout one another; through a certain mutual opposition, they restrain each other to a state of moderation. From this blending, a type of **Temperament** <term>Temperamenti: Also known as "complexion," this is the specific balance of qualities that determines the nature of a living thing or substance.</term> is produced, which is diffused through the entire mass of the **Composite**. 

To this **Temperament**, **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was the Roman physician whose theories of humors and qualities dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> ascribed the causes of all **natural faculties**. He passed down a most shameful error: the claim that the unique property of every single thing arises from this or that balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. 

It is worthwhile to examine these foundations upon which the entirety of **Galenic Medicine** is built. For, deriving the principles of actions, the causes of diseases, and the powers of remedies from this source with a "concise subtlety," they have established an Art that is arrogant in its superficial outline of Methods. 

First, therefore, since **Mixture** <term>Mixtio: The process of substances chemically or physically joining to form a new whole.</term> is a type of motion, it was necessary to include a "mover." For nothing happens without a cause. If they claim the Elements move themselves toward Mixture, we will then ask by what authority they grant such powers to their Elements; for simple motions are suited to simple bodies.

**Balsam**, **Mummy**, clothed in opportune **Stars**, <note>original: "Astris opportunis." Meanwhile, once the signatures and parts are completed, they can safely come forth into the light.

Because this matter flows with great familiarity alongside the spirits and seminal Tinctures, and so clearly demonstrates in the **Anatomy of the testicles** all the symptoms that happen during the flowering of the seeds, it has misled many to believe that the entire power of the seed is contained in this [organ] alone. ### PHILOSOPHICAL STUDIES.

...they are transformed. Hippocrates followed this divine administration of **Generation** with a learned and profound interpretation in his booklet *On Diet*. There, he also proposed the general nature of all **Generations** and **seeds**, which we have previously explained according to his own mind. We shall remove any obscurity through this explanation and shall record the passage here for the reasons mentioned above. After Hippocrates had shown the progression of seeds from **Orcus** <note>original: "ex Orco." In this context, "Orcus" (the Roman underworld) refers to the hidden, unmanifest state of life before it emerges into the light of the world.</note> into the **Light**, and had declared the flow of **Generations** and **Corruptions** through universal doctrine, he descended to the **Nature of man**, saying: *All other things, both the soul of man and the body, the soul itself arranges.* <note>original Greek: "Τὰ δ' ἄλλα πάντα καὶ ψυχὴ ἀνθρώπου καὶ σῶμα ὁποῖον ἡ ψυχὴ διακοσμέεται."</note> This means: *And all other things, and the Soul of man; but the body is fashioned in agreement with the Soul, etc.*

Those vital **Principles**, **radical Tinctures**, and **Mechanical spirits** <term>Mechanical spirits: The "master-builder" forces that follow a divine blueprint to construct the physical body.</term>—in which **Knowledge**, life, and power flourish—he calls the **soul** <note>original Greek: "ψυχὴν" (psyche)</note>; elsewhere he calls it **heat** <note>original Greek: "θερμὸν" (thermon)</note>, as in his book *On Fleshes*, and here he often calls it **fire** <note>original Greek: "πῦρ" (pyr)</note>. He asserts that whatever the **Knowledge** and **Gifts** of these vital spirits, **Soul**, heat, and fire may be, such **signatures** are expressed in the bodies, and the entire decoration of those bodies is contained within the **Soul**. 

Thus the **Soul** is the **Principle** of the organic body: for the body flows from it. By the virtue of the Soul, the **Elements** and **Principles** are mixed and increased; they are changed from spiritual things into corporeal things. They are clothed in shapes, sizes, colors, and similar "paintings" that are agreeable to the **Soul**—that is, those qualities which are worthwhile for fulfilling their **predestined duties**. *And it [the soul] enters into man...* <note>original Greek: "Ἐσέρπει δὲ εἰς ἄνθρωπον."</note>

Foreign things—that is, those which are not *of a like manner* <note>original Greek: "ὁμότροπα" (homotropa), meaning having the same character or habits.</note>—are driven out from alien seats. ## CHAPTER XII.

In the contemplation of natural things, which we have treated until now, we have often had the Philosophers as companions. For by the service of the senses, with a small amount of observation added, the origins of plants and animals can be discovered, and they possess manifest seeds. But indeed, the explanation of diseases—because they have obtained more hidden seeds, and because their **Generations** and **Transplantations** <note>original: "Generationes Transplantationesq"; in this context, "transplantation" refers to how a disease takes root in the body and spreads, similar to how a plant is moved to new soil.</note> are hidden in the **workshop of Nature** <term>Workshop of Nature: A common metaphor in early modern science (alchemy and vitalism) describing the internal, invisible processes where matter is transformed.</term>, subject neither to the judgments of the senses nor to the proud decrees of **syllogisms** <note>A syllogism is a form of logical reasoning (if A=B and B=C, then A=C). The author is criticizing scholars who try to use logic to explain medicine instead of observation and spiritual insight.</note>—is clearly intricate and understood by few.

The **Aristotelians** ascribed diseases to the "family of Privations," <term>Privations: In Aristotelian philosophy, a 'privation' is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present. For example, blindness is the privation of sight.</term> as if they were defects and errors of Nature, in which neither forms, nor differences, nor essences could be found. The **Platonists**, after they were deprived of **Ideas** <note>Platonic "Ideas" or "Forms" were the perfect, eternal blueprints of things. Plato famously struggled with whether "base" or "bad" things like mud, hair, or disease had their own perfect Forms.</note> (for they granted Ideas neither to defects nor to evils), fearing lest they depart too far from the beauty of Beings, left the contemplation of diseases barren; they were mindful of the precept of Plato, who commands those descending [the ladder of knowledge], when they have reached the **Particulars**, to leave them and concede them to infinity <note>original: "Singularia... infinitati concedere." This refers to the idea that science should focus on universal truths, while individual, specific cases (singulars) are too numerous and chaotic to be studied scientifically.</note>.

But the **Physicians**, to whom this province was especially committed, because they had lost the patronage of the Philosophers, being content primarily with observations, left the essence and nature of diseases as something uninvestigable among **Transcendental** things <note>original: "Transcendentalia." Here, it refers to things that lie outside the standard categories of logic and physical classification, making them "unknowable" to the traditional doctor.</note>.

Therefore, they diligently noted what types of illnesses followed from which antecedent causes; and finally, by reducing the immense variety of causes to certain orders, they attempted to derive skillful predictions, preventions, and cures from them. Hence, in the works of **Hippocrates** <note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE) is often called the "Father of Medicine." This text is analyzing his method of clinical observation.</note>, various distinctions of diseases are seen, based on the **efficient causes** <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; here, it refers to the direct trigger of a disease.</note> from which they proceed. In the book *On the Nature of Man*, he says: some diseases arise from the **Diet** <note>original: "Diæta"; in ancient medicine, this referred to a person’s entire lifestyle, including food, drink, exercise, and sleep.</note> which a person uses; others from the **spirit** <note>original: "fpiritu"; here meaning the air we breathe. The ancients believed "miasma" or corrupted air caused widespread epidemics.</note> which we draw in. He adds the signs: when a great many people are seized by one disease at the same time, they are generated by a most common cause, such as the spirit; but when various diseases occupy different people, they happen because of Diet. In the same way, in the book *On Winds*, he distinguishes **fevers** as the most common diseases: affirming some to be common, which proceed from the Air or spirit—I mean spirit defiled by morbid excretions—while others are private, which received the beginnings of their origin from Diet.

In the short book *On Humors*, he says: Some diseases are innate, which one may learn by questioning the patients themselves; others come from the region; some from Diet; and certain others from the constitutions of the seasons. In the first book *On Diseases*, and similarly in the book <margin>On Affections <note>original Greek: περι παθων (Peri pathon)</note></margin> *On Affections* right at the beginning, he says that all diseases happen to men from **Bile** and **Phlegm** <term>Bile and Phlegm: Two of the four "humors" (along with blood and black bile) believed to govern health. An imbalance was thought to cause all illness.</term>, as if they were [already] existing in the body; but these are excited by foods, drinks, labors, heat that over-warms, cold that over-cools, and dry...

A school of ancient doctors who believed medicine should be based on observation and experience rather than hidden causes.</note>, following **Hippocrates**, collected the occurrences of causes, diseases, and symptoms. Through long experience, they noted the notable differences in each class of illness and faithfully communicated these records to their students. 

**Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), perhaps the most influential physician in Roman history, whose work blended philosophy and medicine.</note>, however, who himself had been trained by Empiric teachers, grew weary of the lengthy nature of the art and the tedious delays of long-term experience. He entered the schools of the **Geometers** <note>Mathematicians and logicians.</note>. There, admiring the vigor of their logical proofs and the efficient brevity of their methods, he began to wonder whether it might be worthwhile to apply the methods of the Geometers to the medical art. After much deliberation, he decided to return to the study of medicine. 

Thus, distinguished by the "miracle" of his **Methods** (a thing then new and unheard of among physicians), he was the first to restore a confused art to a systematic order. He confirmed doubtful matters by the law of **Demonstration** <note>Logical or mathematical proof.</note>; nevertheless, he everywhere conceded that the observations and experiences of Hippocrates were valid and stable, as it was necessary to have these as the basic principles for his proofs. Indeed, Galen pursues this narrative and history of himself extensively in almost all of his books. 

Because the nature of diseases had not been sufficiently explained by the Empirics or even by Hippocrates himself, and although the differences noted were plentiful, they were presented by everyone in a confused manner, Galen brought aid to this obscurity through marvelous investigation and a subtle **Method**. <meta>This page continues the technical discussion of Galen’s medical logic, specifically how he organized the causes of disease into four categories and the subsequent challenges to this system by later Renaissance physicians like Fernel.</meta>

-># PHILOSOPHICAL [MATTERS]<-

In his books on *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "Methodi medendi," one of Galen’s most important works on clinical practice.</note>, Galen proposed four distinct classes of things: **Actions**, the **Immediate Causes** of those actions, **Antecedent Causes**, and **Evident** or **External Causes**. He argued that disease must necessarily be contained within these categories. Having excluded the others, he demonstrated that diseases reside specifically in the Immediate Causes of actions. These Immediate Causes are the *diatheses* <note>A Greek term for a physical state or predisposition.</note>, the constitutions, or the physical dispositions of the body's parts. He taught that these are maintained through the proper temperament, shape, and unity of the **Elements**; where there is symmetry, health is produced, but where there is a lack of proportion (*ametria*), diseased actions are the result. Next, he asserted that the **Antecedent Causes** <note>Factors already present in the body that predispose it to illness, such as an imbalance of the four humors.</note> of diseases are contained within the humors. For this reason, he excluded phlegm, bile, melancholy, blood, and the undeservedly named *synovia* <note>original: "synoviam," a term for joint fluid; the author likely considers it an "unnatural" addition to the list of primary body parts.</note> from the count of actual body parts. 

Behold the failure of these sensory-based Methods when faced with the hidden labor <note>original: "lithurgia," from the Greek for service or work.</note> of Nature. For even now, it remains misunderstood within the school of Galen what the **Elements** truly are, how they are mixed, and whether the causes of all actions actually arise from the temperament of these Elements. 

**Fernelius** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a French physician who was one of the first to challenge Galenic orthodoxy and is credited with naming "physiology."</note> certainly confirms that the **Total Substance** <note>original: "totam Substantiam." Fernel argued that some diseases affect the very essence of an organ, not just its elemental balance of hot/cold or wet/dry.</note>, the essential Form, and the hidden property are something distinct from the Elements, and possess a more divine origin. Thus, he established new categories of "similar" diseases <note>Diseases affecting simple tissues like bone or membrane, rather than complex organs.</note>—namely, those of the **Form** or of the **Total Substance**. Within this family of diseases, he placed the *venereal plague* <note>original: "luem veneream," the 16th-century term for syphilis.</note>. 

**Fracanzanus of Vicenza** <note>Antonio Fracanzano, a conservative 16th-century Italian medical professor who defended Galen against these new ideas.</note> lived and died buried in these Galenic qualities; with great severity, he detested those innovators who introduced the names of "hidden properties" and "Total Substance"...

When these are consumed, and their separation and expulsion from the body fail, the sticky mucilages pile up—whether in the stomach, intestines, mesenteric veins <note>the veins connecting the intestines to the abdominal wall and liver</note>, liver, kidneys, bladder, or any other cavity. These are the **subalternate Genera** <note>Intermediate categories in a hierarchy.</note>. 

But when these substances are intensified <note>original: *exaltantur*</note>, and by their volume and consistency they block the passages and become known to people through the destruction caused by their symptoms, they are the **Individual and final Species**. Meanwhile, the impaired or blocked bodily functions are the **Individuals** in the progression of these causes. 

Thus, the fate of **Genera** and **Species** in this classification was unequal. For although the Species and subalternate Genera were contained within the body, they remained hidden and did not display any perceptible condition to the **Atomists** <note>A term likely referring here to medical thinkers who focused on physical particles or matter, as opposed to the traditional four humors.</note> within the body. Consequently, they lost their specific titles and were merely assigned to the collective of **Antecedent Causes**. 

However, the **Individual Species**—also called the lowest, final, or proximate species (by whatever name one prefers)—show a physical condition that is obvious through the clear **impairment of actions** <term>actionum laesione <note>A standard medical phrase referring to the functional failure of an organ or limb.</note></term>...

They derived the name of "Obstruction" from a certain resemblance. For the *Atomists* <note>Followers of ancient theories—revived in the Renaissance—who believed the world was made of tiny particles. We shall reveal their errors more clearly later; for now, we are acting as *Logicians* <note>The author means he is currently focusing on the formal classification and naming of things rather than their physical nature.</note>. For this reason, obstructions are classified among "instrumental diseases" <term>instrumentary diseases <note>In traditional medicine, these are diseases affecting the "instruments" or organs of the body (their shape, size, or position) rather than just the balance of fluids.</note></term>.

The name "Obstruction" holds the status of a Species. However, those substances that are mucilaginous, aluminous, vitriolated <note>containing sulfates or "vitriol"</note>, stony, clay-like, arsenical, antimonial, and sulfurous—or according to *Galen* <note>The 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories of humors dominated medicine for 1,500 years.</note>, those that are phlegmatic or melancholic—and are found in the stomach, liver, mesentery, kidneys, bladder, veins, muscles, membranes, etc., are the Individuals or the most immediate Species.

And just as *Hippocrates* said in his work *On Nourishment*: "Nourishment that is not nourishment: if it is not possible to be nourished, it is nourishment in name, but not in deed; but where it performs the deed, it is nourishment in deed, and not just in name" <note>original Greek: τροφὴ ἡ τροφὴ, ἢν μὴ οἷον τε ἦ τρέφεσθαι, ὄνομα τροφὴ, ἔργον δὲ οὐχὶ: ἔργον τροφὴ, ὄνομα δὲ οὐχὶ</note>. That is to say: food is not food if it cannot nourish; it is an empty name without the action and the underlying substance. But if it demonstrates its destined work through nutrition, it is truly food and not an empty name. We shall say the same regarding Obstruction: "Obstruction is not Obstruction." For if something is discovered in the order of causes that is endowed with power and action, and to which the name of Obstruction applies, then it is a "deed" Obstruction. But if no such thing is seen, the name is empty.

We will now demonstrate a twofold order in the progression of diseases. The *first is the Real order*, based on the coordination and series of efficient causes...

In the womb and at the very start of our creation <note>original: "Generationum initiis"</note>, the first necessity is for these spirits, which are drawn in through the service of hidden respiration and the pulse. Although this nourishment is invisible, and is not marked by the **signatures** <term>outward physical signs or "stamps" on a natural object that reveal its inner properties or medicinal uses</term> or qualities used to distinguish the foods of the lower globe <note>the terrestrial realm</note>, it is nevertheless not without its own appropriate and proper signatures.
