<page-num>294</page-num>

### IDEA OF MEDICINE
<meta>catchword: fevers</meta>

In certain diseases, the investigation is not difficult, such as in those which occupy the **anatomies** <term>anatomies<gloss>In this context, the term refers to the internal structures or regional systems of specific organs where disease manifestations occur.</gloss></term> of the stomach, intestines, kidneys, liver, and mesentery—especially if they arise from **tartaric mucilages** <term>tartaric mucilages<gloss>Viscous or slimy substances that harden into stony deposits; a core concept in Paracelsian medicine, comparing human disease to the "tartar" (sediment) that crusts inside a wine barrel.</gloss></term>. For burning sensations and erosions of the stomach—called **Orexes** <note>original: *Orexes*; a Paracelsian term for a type of burning, acidic hunger or irritation.</note> by **Paracelsus**—compressions of the chest, and symptoms close to these, such as nausea, vomiting, loathing of food, belching, bloating, and sluggishness, indicate that the morbid **roots** <note>original: *radices*; the underlying causal origins.</note> are contained within the anatomy of the stomach.

Colic pains; compressions or obstructions of the liver, spleen, and mesentery; and **orexes** or colics of the kidneys and bladder—that is, **dysuria** <gloss>difficulty or pain in passing urine</gloss>, **stranguria** <gloss>painful, drop-by-drop urination</gloss>, stones, sand, clumps, and so on—possess easy diagnoses. For they immediately indicate the **minerals** <note>original: *Mineras*; the internal "mines" or sites where disease-substances accumulate and grow.</note> in which they are fostered, because they consist of **seeds** whose fruits are destined for **coagulation** <gloss>the process by which fluid substances in the body harden into physical matter, such as stones or obstructions.</gloss>. 

They also possess slow generations, and by the immobile and sluggish presence of their fruits, they signify a slow nature of the roots—whether they maintain a continuity of time in the resolution of their fruits, or, having broken that continuity, they fulfill nature’s debt through repeated **paroxysms** <gloss>sudden, intense fits or attacks of a disease.</gloss>. 

However, those diseases which consist of lighter, mobile, and not-so-fixed impurities—whose fruits do not end in such thick and immobile coagulations, whose generation is sudden, and whose impressions are swift and penetrating through all things—are discovered with difficulty, even though they often have their **matrices** <term>matrices<gloss>The environments or "wombs" (such as a specific organ) where a disease-seed is nourished and develops.</gloss></term> in the aforementioned "anatomies." The **consensus and sympathy** <note>original: *Consensus & sympathia*; the ancient medical theory that organs can affect one another through shared "feeling" or biological connection.</note> of the body's parts increases this difficulty. <summary>This page explains that "tartaric" diseases—those involving physical deposits like stones or blockages in the organs—are easily diagnosed because they grow slowly and leave clear evidence. In contrast, diseases caused by "lighter" or mobile impurities are harder to detect because they move quickly through the body and lack physical coagulation.</summary>

<header>### PHILOSOPHICAL MEDICINE</header>

Tertian, daily, quartan, continuous, false, erratic, and even hectic fevers (forgive Paracelsus, spirits of Galen <note>original: *manes Galeni*; a reference to the 2nd-century physician Galen, whose theories Paracelsus famously rejected.</note>) can have their fuel sources in the stomach, intestines, the veins of the mesentery, the liver, spleen, and kidneys. For this reason, they are not easily discerned, because during the silent intervals between attacks, for the most part, no manifest symptoms of those parts remain from which rational conjectures about the suspected **anatomies** <term>anatomies<gloss>Internal structures or regional systems of specific organs where disease takes root.</gloss></term> might be drawn. During the onset of **paroxysms** <gloss>sudden attacks or peaks of fever</gloss>, all parts of the body are suddenly drawn into sympathy, because the febrile breakdowns infect the vital elements of our body with **Cherionian Tinctures** <note>original: *Tincturis Cherionijs*; a term derived from the centaur Chiron, referring to the essential qualities or "medicines" of the body.</note>—that is, those marked by the properties of the **Three Principles** <note>In Paracelsian theory, these are Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, the three fundamental substances of all matter.</note>.

Furthermore, if helleborine impurities <gloss>purging or irritating substances related to the hellebore plant</gloss> are contained in the stomach, colic ones in the intestines, bituminous <gloss>sticky or tar-like</gloss> ones in the mesentery, liver, or spleen, or tartaric <gloss>stony or sedimentary</gloss> ones in the kidneys, they will all be irritated by the impressions and breakdowns of the febrile Tinctures. They will leave symptoms after the paroxysms in harmless places—that is, in locations where the febrile **roots** <note>original: *radices*; the underlying causal origins.</note> are not actually fostered.

Hence, nausea, loathing of food, vomiting, compressions of the stomach, liver, and spleen, and colic, back, and kidney pains appear during fevers; and these are often left behind during the quiet periods between paroxysms, even though the roots of the fevers may lie hidden in other seats. This argues against the suspect ease of those aphorisms used in investigating the **mines of diseases** <note>original: *mineris morborum*; the internal sites where disease-substances accumulate.</note>: *Where there is pain, there is the disease; where there is swelling, there is the disease,* and so on.

# THE CONCEPT OF MEDICINE

Because the question concerns the locations of **seeds** <note>original: "seminum"; in Paracelsian medicine, seeds are the formative principles that grow into either healthy organs or specific diseases.</note> and bodies, we shall remove ambiguity and obscurity with a brief explanation. Therefore, according to the difference and connection of things, there will also be a diversity in their "place of being." A rotten and rancid trunk, or a dead stone devoid of vital spirit, is said to be "in the earth" in a very different way than a tree fixed into the earth by its roots and fibers, drawing nourishment from it as if from a **womb** <note>original: "matrice"</note>. In such cases, the "minerals" <note>The foundational chemical or spiritual sources.</note> and the **matrices** <note>The "wombs" or formative environments.</note> of the **Roots** are found only with the greatest difficulty.

They have no proportion or relevance to the seeds and the properties of the seeds from which the aforementioned diseases are derived. 

Indeed, in **epilepsy**, when the affected location is sought, no pains, no specific site, no excrement, and no tumors appear. Therefore, based solely on the **impaired action** <term>actione læsa<gloss>A standard Galenic diagnostic principle: if a function (like walking or thinking) is broken, the organ responsible for that function must be the site of the disease.</gloss></term> (specifically of the "animal" or soulful functions), Galen concludes—and the **Galenists** <note>The traditionalist followers of Galen's medical system.</note> affirm—that the **fuel of the disease** <note>original: *fomitem morbi*; the source or "tinder" that feeds the illness.</note> is in the **ventricles of the brain**, and especially in the posterior ones. 

I wonder why they have not placed it in the **heart**. For the actions of the heart are impaired just as much as those of the brain. They otherwise seem insensitive toward the heart, forcibly situating the invisible lodgings of so many and such diverse **fevers** within it.

From this arise infinite errors, follies, and miseries, because the explanations of diseases are confused and wrongly described based only on the evidence of outward symptoms. 

For example, because in fevers the **heart** seemed to be primarily affected by an imbalance of heat, they neglected the true roots of fevers. It is from the vaporous resolutions of these roots that not only heat, but also chills and all the various symptoms of fevers proceed. Instead, they simply declared that a fever is a "heat kindled in the heart." Had they claimed instead that a coldness was introduced into the heart, they would have been just as well-fortified by the conjectures of their **Analogisms**...

...they proceed from invisible things, and are known to only a few, as their slowness and rarity increase the difficulty of understanding them. In all these matters, one may observe a twofold timing: that of **Digestions** <term>Digestion: In this context, it refers to the internal ripening or "cooking" of a substance by natural heat until it reaches maturity.</term> or maturities, and that of **Resolutions** <term>Resolution: The stage where a substance breaks forth, dissolves into its final form, or releases its "fruit."</term>. For these differ greatly from one another: not everything that has a slow period of digestion will also show a slow resolution of its fruits. 

The times of **Digestion** are continuous in all things; but the times of **Resolution** are, in many cases, interrupted. **Metals** have long periods of Digestion. # PHILOSOPHICAL LESSONS

<page-num>319</page-num>

The logic of **critical days** <note>original: "cretoriorum dierum." In traditional medicine, these were specific days during an illness (like the 7th or 14th) when a "crisis" was expected to occur, determining the patient's fate.</note> will be demonstrated with great ease. The biological power believed to drive out disease-causing substances.</note>.

Nor is it necessary to seek out the physical forms and external **signatures** <note>original: "signaturas." The "Doctrine of Signatures" was the belief that plants look like the body parts they are meant to heal—for example, a heart-shaped leaf for heart disease. The author is arguing against this literal interpretation.</note> of natural things within the **Anatomy** of the **Microcosm** <note>original: "Microcosmi." The human being, viewed as a miniature version of the entire universe.</note>. Instead, the **properties**, **Sciences**, **Gifts**, **predestinations**, **seminal Tinctures** <note>original: "Tincturæ." The essential, concentrated spirit or medicinal power of a substance.</note>, and the guardians of life and power are enough. It is useless to look for an ox, a cypress, a beech, wheat, a vine, gold, or an emerald inside a human being. But anyone who seeks the **properties** and **radical Tinctures**—the sources of all actions—of grapes, wheat, barley, gold, emeralds, roses, and violets, will find them.

Nor will one find the properties of these things alone; in some cases, one will detect the qualities of **vitriol**, **sulfur**, **nitre**, **mercury**, **arsenic**, **antimony**, **monkshood**, **nettle**, **arum** <note>A genus of flowering plants, often called "cuckoopint."</note>, **opium**, **mandrake**, and **hemlock**. Indeed, the seeds of natural things are **resolved** <note>original: "resoluta." Broken down into their basic, spiritual, or chemical essence.</note> and made spiritual during the **generations** and **transmutations** within the **Microcosm**. Having clarified <note>The catchword from the previous page was "bus," completing the word "claratis" (clarified).</note> these matters, we shall briefly and without offense undertake a critique of the various **Indications** <term>Indications: signs or symptoms that suggest a specific medical treatment is necessary</term>. Cures that are performed by the service of the hands—such as the resetting of dislocated limbs, the appropriate bandaging of fractures, incisions, cauterization <note>original: ustiones; the practice of burning tissue to close a wound or remove a growth</note>, bloodletting, **scarifications** <term>scarification: the practice of making small, shallow cuts in the skin, often used in conjunction with cupping</term>, and similar operations—are clearly artificial and external. These are to be completed by bodily agility, practice, and habit, rather than by the power of Nature.

Ailments or the injuries caused by diseases that yield to these treatments are external and subject to the senses. In these cases, the methods of acting are suggested by the common judgment of the senses; that is, the **Indications** are evident even to unlearned country folk. However, it is the skill, habit, and practice of performing the intended task that makes the craftsmen. These craftsmen, driven by the stings of vanity and greed, often abuse their duties—cutting, burning, and extracting where there was no need for cutting, burning, or extraction.

Because, however, symptoms such as inflammations, ulcerations, pains, and **discharges** <note>original: fluxiones; in traditional medicine, this refers to the movement of harmful "humors" or fluids to a specific part of the body</note> often follow upon fractures, bruises, and dislocations, physicians understood that repositioning or bandaging alone was not enough, but that there was a need for remedies and the assistance of Nature. In these symptoms, the causes were obscure, and the methods of acting were not immediately demonstrated by the external senses and naked guesswork. Therefore, through a more subtle inquiry, they either sought the causes and origins of the symptoms themselves, or learned them from their predecessors—

### IDEA OF MEDICINE

-> The Balsam of the Microcosm <-

**Particular** [healing] is that in which the roots themselves, or the **seminal Tinctures** <term>seminal Tinctures: the internal "seeds" or essential spiritual causes of a disease</term> of diseases are not always removed. Instead, more often the "fruits," symptoms, paroxysms, and pains are mitigated or prevented; they are not permitted to reach their **exaltations** <term>exaltations: the highest peak of intensity or most refined state of a disease or substance</term>. In these cases, the evacuation of excrements is established, and strengthening measures for a weakened nature are added. Such cures have degrees, higher and lower, according as they more closely approach or recede from the properties and conditions of **Universal** cures. They are classified as Generic, Subalternate, Specific, or Individual, by reason of their degrees and properties. 

For these three things—Diseases, Remedies, and Healing—possess consistent and reciprocal analogies, especially the remedy and the cure. Accordingly, differences in remedies give birth to varieties of cures, and the natures of diseases—their peaks, locations, and generations—demonstrate the orders of cures and remedies, and vice versa. 

Thus, **hereditary diseases** <note>original: *morbi hereditarij*</note>, when they have reached their peaks, and also other fully-formed diseases—such as **epilepsy** <note>original: *epilepsiæ*</note>, **gout** <note>original: *podagræ*</note>, **leprosy** <note>original: *lepræ*</note>, and **dropsy** <note>original: *hydropes*; swelling from fluid retention</note>—require Universal healing and perfect remedies. Therefore, if we are not permitted to reach the Universal cures, we would certainly be blessed if we could at least attain the **Particular**, Subalternate, Specific, and Individual types of cures. By "Particular" cures, I mean those which nevertheless legitimately imitate the conditions and properties of that Universal and highest cure as much as possible; those which, leaving behind the infinite variety of individual cases, focus on the **Species** and the higher **Genera**...

### IDEA OF MEDICINE

...whatever settles hunger: and such things are foods. Again, drink heals thirst. Now, we have said before that thirst is the same as the desired liquid or drink, just as nourishment is the same as that which is intended to nourish. Therefore, when **PARACELSUS** says, *Like is cured by like* <note>original Latin: "Similia Similibus curari"</note>, he is not insane, nor does he speak foolishly; rather, he perceives rightly and speaks as a philosopher. He does not oppose **Hippocrates**, who asserted that hunger is cured by food, thirst by drink, fullness by evacuation, emptiness by replenishment, labor by rest, rest by labor, and so on—and universally, that *Opposites are the remedies for opposites* <note>original Latin: "Contraria Contrariorum esse remedia"</note>. This means Medicine is nothing other than the addition of those things which are desired and the removal of those things which are redundant.

However, **Paracelsus** clearly opposes **Galen**, who primarily applies this "Hippocratic Opposition" to those bare qualities <note>The four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> which were actually condemned by Hippocrates in his book *On Ancient Medicine*. For Galen refers the primary and principal **Ideas of Cures** to cooling, heating, moistening, and drying, and the various combinations of these. Following him, the **Arabs** and modern Physicians have become heaters and bath-attendants <note>The author uses "Balneatores" (bath-attendants) as a derogatory term for doctors who only use temperature-based treatments like baths or heating pads rather than chemical medicine.</note> rather than true Healers...

From this, remedies for diseases are called "similars" because they are derived from the same **Anatomy of Nature** <note>In this context, the "Anatomy of Nature" is not the dissection of corpses, but the study of the inner chemical and spiritual structures that link the natural world to the human body.</note>, for they contain similar **signatures** <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" is the belief that God or Nature marked every medicinal substance with a physical sign—such as a shape or color—that indicates its use.</note>, properties, and roots. Rather, it is because that heat is also bitter and hot, or sharp, pungent and hot, or salty and hot, and because infinite other faculties are mixed with the heat. For from a single root, seed, or impurity flow the signatures <term>signatures: the outward physical signs—like color, taste, or shape—that reveal a substance's inner medicinal purpose</term> of colors, flavors, odors, shapes, coagulations, and similar traits—just as we have often explained before.

In the same way, cold is joined to other powers. Therefore, in diseases, it is the Powers—because they more closely reflect the properties of the roots—that are the "authors" of the symptoms. Saltiness, bitterness, pungency, sharpness, and harshness possess Powers and inflict pains; meanwhile, heats, drynesses, colds, and moistures merely concur, sharpening and increasing the effects of the Powers. However, these [four qualities] possess no Power marked by a radical property or inherent intelligence <note>original: "scientia"</note>. 

With a copious demonstration drawn from the method of curing, the generation of diseases, and other signs, **Hippocrates** himself, in the aforementioned place, confounds the Galenic theorems (which themselves suffer from imbalance <note>original: "intemperie laborantia" — a play on words, as "intemperie" usually refers to a bodily imbalance, but here refers to the flaws in Galen's logic</note>). And I wonder why **Galen** did not relegate that little book <note>Hippocrates' "On Ancient Medicine"</note> to the category of illegitimate or forged works, since it so clearly and diametrically fights against his entire system of medicine. This will become even clearer in the Paraphrase of that same...

# THE IDEA OF MEDICINE
### Page 378

...we have revealed the book of Hippocrates. In soothing pains and fevers <note>original: "caloribus," literally "heats"</note>, these [conventional physicians] have one remedy in common with true Physicians: namely, bloodletting <term>bloodletting: the surgical practice of "opening a vein" (venae sectio) to withdraw blood, then believed to balance the body's humors</term>. If they were deprived of this, they would be utterly hopeless. Yet, it does not have a place in all pains or fevers. Often, through the harmful loss of the highest quality blood, fevers are removed that would have more successfully yielded to more timely remedies, without injury or the draining of other parts of the body.

They are also overwhelmed by a multitude of indications <term>indications: signs or symptoms that point a physician toward a specific treatment</term>. They derive these from "Antecedent" causes, "Containing" causes <note>In Scholastic medicine, "antecedent" causes were external factors like diet, while "containing" causes were the internal states directly producing the disease</note>, from the diseases themselves, and sometimes from the symptoms. They deduce indications that are agreeing, conflicting, preceding, following, and cohering with a marvelous—if unnecessary—subtlety. 

The sick are stunned by the outcome of such a harsh struggle, especially if the difficult displays of the physicians' "preludes" <note>original: "Prooemiorum," referring to the elaborate diagnostic speeches physicians gave at the bedside to impress patients</note> offer firm prophecies of the future. Thus, they immediately rush to treat the more urgent or dangerous symptom, disease, condition, or cause, even if by doing so they harm the state of other parts of the body. In this way, pains are mitigated while the diseases—and the causes of those diseases—actually increase. Causes are removed while the patient's current strength is neglected.

<page-num>372</page-num>
<header>THE IDEA OF MEDICINE</header>

...proposed to cure. They will say that they strive to achieve concoctions <note>The process of "cooking" or ripening raw, diseased humors so the body can expel them.</note> through syrups and decoctions. This will certainly not be achieved by syrups that are "cutting," thinning, opening, honey-vinegar based <note>original: *oxymelliticis*</note>, squill-based <note>original: *scylliticis*; syrups made from the sea onion, used as an expectorant or diuretic</note>, or those made of roots and similar things. For those substances that must be ripened <note>original: *maturanda*</note>, it is necessary to enclose them within, to thicken them, and to temper them.

With syrups of rose, violet, maidenhair fern <note>original: *capillorum veneris*</note>, and licorice, they will indeed achieve concoctions, mitigations, and temperings in certain lighter diseases—namely those involving catarrhs <note>excessive discharge of mucus</note> or those adhering superficially to the stomach or other parts. But indeed, in such diseases, ripening treatments are not required. It is permissible to immediately provide purgatives or resolving agents; for these impurities are superficial and easily moved.

Hippocrates himself explained what concoction is and by what means it is accomplished in his book *On Ancient Medicine*, saying: Τὸ πεφθῆναι γίνεται ἐκ τοῦ μιχθῆναι κρηθῆναι καὶ ἀλλήλοισι συνεψηθῆναι <note>original Greek: "Concoction occurs from being mixed, blended, and boiled together with one another."</note>. That is to say: Concoctions are perfected from the mixing, tempering, and mutual digestion of mixed things. For in this way, the sharpness of the humors' powers is softened, the extremes and excesses are tempered, and pains, fevers <note>original: *calores*, literally "heats"</note>, and all symptoms are alleviated. 

Therefore, these curative indications are equivalent: to cure through "Mitigatives" according to **PARACELSUS**, through "Concoctions" according to Hippocrates, and through <term>Epicrasis</term> <note>A Galenic term for a treatment that alters or tempers the humors gradually rather than evacuating them all at once.</note> according to Galen. Nor are these necessary in the treatment of all diseases, as we have said before.

<page-num>371</page-num>
<header>PHILOSOPHICAL MATTERS</header>
<sig>AA 3</sig>

...we argue that in diseases consisting of mobile and superficial impurities that have not struck deep roots—such as most fevers, catarrhs <note>excessive discharge of mucus</note>, coughs, hoarseness, and similar conditions—there is no need for these medical "Indications" <note>Formal rules used by physicians to decide on a course of treatment</note>. They are safely and suddenly removed by the help of purgatives <note>medicines used to evacuate the bowels</note> or cleansing agents.

On the other hand, more violent and dangerous conditions—such as certain fevers and abscesses <note>original: *apostemata*; localized collections of pus</note> in which the breakdown of impurities is mobile, easily yielding, and not destined for difficult "coagulations" <note>the process of fluids thickening or hardening into a diseased state</note>—can also admit purgations even at their onset. This state is identified by the "signatures" <note>distinctive signs or marks</note> of the pains and by the inconsistent and swollen "effervescences" <note>sudden flare-ups or boiling over of bodily fluids</note> of the symptoms. By the effectiveness of these purgatives, the burning and mobile impurities of the diseases are often removed, rendering the later duties of concoction <note>the process of ripening diseased matter for expulsion</note> superfluous.

But indeed, feverish and inflammatory impurities that possess more difficult "Tinctures" <note>original: *Tincturas*; here referring to deeply ingrained qualities or "dyes" that alter the body’s state</note>, and whose breakdowns and vapors allow for fixed "coagulations" that are difficult to resolve (such things are constantly received in the suspected parts and corresponding "minerals" <note>original: *mineris*; likely referring to the internal chemical sources or "seeds" of disease within the organs</note>), are most safely cured through **Epicrasis** <note>the gradual evacuation of humors in small amounts</note>, **Concoction**, or **Mitigation**.

For these do not yield to the raw properties of common purgative medicines, which act upon bodily and raw "spirits" <note>the subtle, active forces within the body</note> and which only aggravate the flare-ups of the diseased spirits. ...they ordered [them] to seek, even with a capon <note>A castrated rooster; old medical recipes often involved boiling herbs or precious stones with meat to "transfer" their virtues</note>, so that the virtues might be more closely joined. ### THE IDEA OF MEDICINE ###

With these same substances, we often restore health to the sick, and we have cut short milder fevers, cases of jaundice, pleurisy, <term>catarrhs<gloss>excessive buildup of mucus in the nose or throat</gloss></term>, and coughs. Therefore, we sought better and more powerful things, more exquisitely prepared and more successfully composed.

Nor shall those famous remedies, which are now praised by some and blamed by others throughout all **Germany**, escape the judgment of these assemblies. Among these, we will first bring forward **glass of antimony** <note>original: *Antimonij uitrum*; a glassy substance produced by melting antimony ore, used as a powerful and often violent emetic</note>. This deserves accusation because it has not admitted the separation of the pure from the impure; because it has not sustained the required resolution and <term>digestion<gloss>the alchemical process of subjecting a substance to gentle, consistent heat to mature it</gloss></term>; and because it has undergone **vitrifying fusion**, which should be avoided in every preparation of remedies.

We require **Spiritual Fusions**, not Corporeal ones. In vain, too, are purgings of the bowels obstinately performed by means of antimony; it was intended for higher <term>predestinations<gloss>a Paracelsian term meaning the specific "destiny" or ultimate healing purpose of a substance</gloss></term>.

This we accept as a useful medicine, necessary in many conditions and cures. ...most useful <note>original: *plurimis*—the first syllable was the catchword on the previous page</note> for many ailments, both internal and external. It is not my intention to list everything now. Anyone who is well-practiced in these examples will be able to form a fair judgment concerning the preparations of most remedies.

There are also other types of remedies which differ from the previous ones in the method of their preparation. For just as <term>Hippocrates<gloss>the ancient Greek physician regarded as the father of medicine</gloss></term> said regarding nourishment: nourishment is that which nourishes—that is, that which has been converted into spiritual vapors, separated from impurities, digested, and matured. For the <term>vital spirits<gloss>the subtle, active substances in the body believed to sustain life and movement</gloss></term>, which are the authors of our actions, are nourished by such vapors. 

Secondly, nourishment is also that which does indeed nourish, but obscurely or equivocally, imitating true nutrition with only a shadowed image; in this case, the refined separation and digestion are not complete. Third, nourishment is that which is *about* to nourish; such a thing exists in a bodily state and is the primary subject that requires resolution, separation, and digestion. 

In this same way, we shall speak of remedies: some remedies heal diseases, others "as if" heal them, and some are "about to" heal. Those which are spiritual and suited to the diseases...

<page-num>105</page-num>
-># CONCLUSION<-

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial "I" at the start of the text, featuring an ornate design of flowing foliage and floral patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

**I** have proposed the vision of **Philosophical Medicine** <note>original: "Philosophicæ Medicinæ"; this refers to a branch of medicine, often associated with Paracelsus, that relied on chemistry and the "inner essence" of things rather than just the four humors</note>, I have laid solid foundations, and from these I have logically derived all the duties of the Art. Frequently joining together the agreement of *Hippocrates* and the ancient philosophers, I have demonstrated that the methods of medicine in which this present age now triumphs are supported by no authority from antiquity. I have frequently explained the causes of errors and their corrections. Truly, I believed that the **Light of Nature** <note>A Renaissance concept referring to the innate human capacity to understand the world through observation and divine inspiration, rather than just reading old books</note> was not exhausted in *Galen* alone, but that seeds of wisdom were still left in the treasuries of knowledge, which by an immutable law are destined for specific times and nations until the end of the age.

Therefore, if Galen—relying on his own freedom of judgment—often disputed frivolously against *Archigenes*, *Asclepiades*, *Herophilus*, *Protagoras*, *Erasistratus*, and *Quintius* his own teacher, and even against *Moses* (the interpreter of living philosophy), what kind of religious obligation is it to venerate his own writings as if they were **Gospel oracles**? Especially when he did not intend them for us any more than he did for bears and boars? What kind of impiety is it to judge *Hippocrates* by the standards of *Galen*, rather than *Galen* by *Hippocrates*? Men ought not to snatch away from other men the freedom of the human intellect, the Light of Nature, and the faculty of discerning and judging. 

The **Monarchy of the Greeks** <note>The total dominance of Greek medical texts, particularly those of Galen, over European universities for over 1,500 years</note> has ended. It is shameful to seek protection for our own sluggishness and laziness from the vigils, labors, and observations of others. I praise *Galen's* industry; I admire the subtlety and speed of his intellect. I also admit the observations which he included—though they were few, uncelebrated, and shaped to fit his own <term>hypotheses<gloss>theoretical frameworks used to explain symptoms</gloss></term>. Nor do I despise all the <term>Indications<gloss>signs that suggest a specific treatment</gloss></term> for cures or the <term>diagnoses<gloss>original: "dignotiones"; the identification of the nature of an illness</gloss></term> of affected areas which he himself proposed. 

I have declared in these commentaries in which diseases and by what reasoning the **Galenic** diagnoses and indications might have a place. Those are mistaken who think we wish to suddenly demolish all the laws of healing received through long custom. It is a safer counsel to correct errors gradually, and to strenuously rouse the industry of physicians toward the investigation of **Nature** and its **Properties**, from which all healings and...

...whereby all vital actions proceed, can be led along secretly; for in this way, their duty will be fulfilled with greater gratitude. Therefore, having been warned, be vigilant; and mindful of your station, investigate the mysteries of Nature with greater diligence. And unless, from this point forward, more just and diligent duties are dear to your heart...

# RECAPITULATION
## CONTAINING THE PRINCIPAL 
## CONCLUSIONS OF THE WHOLE OF PHILO-
## SOPHICAL MEDICINE,
*according to the order preserved in the previous Chapters.*

The medicine for all diseases was created by the Most High <note>original: "Altissimo"; a common reference to God as the creator of natural remedies</note> and placed within Nature. When it is properly prepared and separated from the Elements <term>Elements: in this context, the four physical states (earth, water, air, fire) that "cloak" the pure medicinal essence</term> and the impurities mixed within them, it can, through its power and vital strength, take away all the ailments of the human body. It does this not by heating, cooling, moistening, or drying <note>the author is rejecting the traditional Galenic method of "contraries," which sought to balance the four humors through these qualities</note>, nor by cleansing, cutting, or penetration, but by a far higher property of actions. It is founded upon the vital Principle—the Seed and the Balsam <term>Balsam: a term used in vitalist medicine to describe an internal, life-preserving liquid or essence that prevents decay and heals wounds</term>—of Plants, Minerals, and Animals. We attribute the beginning of all actions in Nature to this principle. Thus, the lawful preparation and administration of this Nature constitutes Medical Science and rightly identifies those who are truly Physicians.

Because, in truth, the foundations of all natural actions are contained in that radical matter, the Balsam, and the vital Sulfur <term>Sulfur: in early chemical philosophy, Sulfur represented the "soul" or the principle of inflammability and growth, one of the three fundamental components of all matter</term>, the Physician must investigate the properties, differences, preparations, and administrations of this Nature with all industriousness, care, and diligence.

The Elements are the locations, matrices <note>original: "matrices"; literally "wombs," implying that the elements act as the maternal environment where life is formed</note>, and dwellings, fortified with a vital and strong power, which nourish the seeds dedicated to Generation, awaken them at the appointed times, and lead them to matu- <note>The text continues on the next page with the word "maturity" (maturitatem)</note>

<summary>This page serves as a summary of the author's medical philosophy, arguing that true medicine is a "vital principle" or "balsam" hidden within nature that must be chemically extracted to heal the body.</summary>

...promote [health] <note>The text begins mid-word, likely "sanitatem" (health) or "utilitatem" (utility)</note>, and grant shelters to those who have served their time <note>original: "emeritis"; a term for retired soldiers, here referring to elements or forces that have fulfilled their natural purpose</note> in a blessed, unchanging rest. Seeds are the bonds of both Natures, joining visible things to invisible things: within them are contained the laws of motions, the predestined timings of events, the sacred duties <note>original: "lithurgiæ"; suggesting that natural processes like growth are a form of divine service</note> of Generation and Transplantation, and the dispensations of the entire worldly Anatomy <term>Anatomy: here referring to the structural arrangement of the entire universe, not just the human body</term>, as if held within vital powers adorned with incomprehensible wisdom.

From these seeds proceed flavors, odors, colors, and all vital qualities, as well as quantities, numbers, shapes, and all other signatures <term>Signatures: the theory that the outward appearance of a plant or mineral indicates its inner medicinal purpose</term> in the mechanical process of Generations and transformations.

Ordered bodies then constitute a **true Mixture**, freed from the dangers of the "penetration of dimensions" <note>original: "penetrationis dimensionum"; a philosophical problem regarding how two physical substances can occupy the same space; the author argues that a true alchemical mixture avoids this paradox</note>; and this is achieved by the vital power of the **mechanical spirits** <term>mechanical spirits: original "spirituum mechanicorum"; these are not "ghosts" but active, semi-material agents or "workmen" of nature that carry out the physical construction of a living body</term>. 

**Transplantation** happens to **Generation** when a **Mixture** intervenes, and it is common to all orders of Generations. With a fertile offspring of **mechanical spirits**, it flows by natural impulse to the anatomy of the testes, and from there to the **womb** <note>original: "matrice"</note>, together with the **seminal matter**, which, prepared in the testes, more happily guards the spiritual Principles.

Finally, the **Signatures** <term>Signatures: original "Signaturae"; the physical characteristics of a plant or substance that reveal its medicinal use</term> and the remaining **Symptoms** <note>original: "symptomata"</note> of diseases—such as impaired bodily functions, changes in waste products, fevers, pains, and colors—arise from the spiritual and vaporous releases of diseased **Roots**.

**Treatments** <note>original: "Curationes"</note> for all diseases are twofold: **Universal** and **Particular**.

In a **Universal** and perfect treatment, a single remedy accomplishes the dissolving of diseased impurities, cleansing, the wearing away or removal of morbid matter, as well as restoration, relief, and the strengthening of the innate **Balsam** <term>Balsam: original "Balasami"; in Paracelsian medicine, the internal life-force or preservative fluid that protects the body from decay and disease</term>.

On the other hand, **Particular** treatments—those that are true and legitimate—are carried out through many **Indications** <note>original: "Indications"; the specific signs that point toward a particular remedy</note> and various properties of remedies; nevertheless, they imitate the actions and conditions of the Universal treatment as much as possible.

True healing **Indications** are founded upon the properties of **Vegetables**, **Minerals**, and **Animals**, and they allow for easy blending when prepared correctly.

The duties of Universal treatments are often fulfilled through Particular Indications and remedies in cases where diseases are not yet advanced or extreme. There are also degrees of **Particular Remedies**, both higher and lower.

Heating, cooling, moistening, and drying treatments <note>These are the four qualities used in traditional Galenic medicine, which the author is criticizing here</note> show only **illusory indications**; they lack the radical properties of Nature, which are the true dispensers of **Science** and power.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of medical theory from page 415. <page-num>416</page-num>

The differences between **Remedies** <note>original: "Remediorum"</note> imitate the very nature of diseases: they encompass simple forms, compositions, powers, and **exaltations** <term>Exaltations: original "exaltationes"; the alchemical process of increasing a substance's potency or "raising" it to a higher state of purity</term> according to the patterns of the illnesses themselves. Remedies are classified as **Nutritional**, **Medicinal**, and **Poisonous**. In each of these types, the same underlying properties are active, yet they differ in their power to act and the strength of their medicinal virtues. **Specific faculties** <note>original: "Specificæ facultates"; the unique healing powers inherent to a particular substance</note> are contained within Nature that are directed toward particular impurities in the body.

Qualities such as heat or cold, tastes, and external applications are unreliable **judges** <note>original: "Cenſores"</note> for determining the true properties of remedies. The fundamental **Principles** <term>Principles: original "Principia"; likely referring to the Paracelsian Tria Prima (Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury) which were thought to be the spiritual "roots" of all physical matter</term> of substances reveal the roots of their properties more accurately. 

Indeed, because there is no reason to avoid the use of **Poisonous** substances in medicine, the necessity for **Preparations** and **Compositions** has arisen. Through these processes, raw substances are "ripened," impurities are separated, and physical matter is dissolved and rendered into a **spiritual** <note>refined, vaporous, or highly distilled</note> form. Harsh heats, tastes, smells, and similar qualities that are harmful to human nature are corrected, softened, or removed, while the curative virtues that heal diseases remain unharmed. 

Combining substances is easier when dealing with **spiritual remedies** than with raw ones, as the need for complex mixing is often eliminated through the preparation process itself. In these preparations, the **Specific Powers** of the medicinal properties are preserved, even if the individual way they act may 
->vary.<-

Are mixed in our **Etna** <note>the volcano in Sicily, used here as a metaphor for the central fire or "laboratory" within the Earth</note>?
Here, where the elder **Vulcan** <note>the god of fire and smithing</note> in starry caves,
And the **Archaeus** <term>Archaeus: the invisible "master craftsman" or vital force that directs the growth and transformation of matter</term> Father, and the rest of the brothers in order,
Forge weapons for Jove and weapons vomiting flames:
Who has enclosed the stable laws, and the volumes of rapid motion,
And the paths of the stars within a fitting limit?

Oh, the shame! Here **Phantasms** <note>original: "Phantasmata"; here meaning mental delusions or false theories</note> delude all the senses.
Not massive Squares, nor Cylinders of vast bulk,
Nor circles within circles, and axes entwined with axes <note>a critique of the complex "epicycles" used in traditional astronomy to calculate planetary paths</note>,
Not the ethereal globe painted with the figures of the signs,
Not Numbers, nor the calculus drawn out by sharp art,
Set free the wits that fail throughout the whole sky.
Nonetheless, they dare no less to attach monstrous **Spheres** to our roofs,
And to add unheard-of masses to the chambers of the Gods
By a desecrating crime.
It is even deemed an honor to have changed the laws
And the signs of the great World: to have wished the **Earth**
To move through the heavens against its will <note>a reference to the Copernican theory that the Earth revolves around the Sun</note>;

To the lowest **Tartarus** <note>the deep abyss of the underworld; here used to describe the Sun being demoted from its central, moving position</note>
Is considered a great thing; many, puffed up with this praise, grow weary.

<meta>This page continues the poetic transition from the previous discussion of the "Crossroads" of medical choice. It moves from the warning of "impure seeds" (false medical theories) to an epic celebration of a new, divinely-ordered medical "Art" that can conquer even the most monstrous diseases. The imagery shifts from the darkness of confusion to the arrival of a long-awaited "Light."</meta>

So that a harmful crop does not rise from impure seed,
And flourish in a foreign field, mixed with the good.
So that, arranged on a certain day, it may flourish
From its deepest roots, and bring forth a sprout from a dire sprout.
Nor is it enough to have learned the hidden causes
Of a shapeless offspring: we are blessed by a better **Fate**. <term>Fata: The predetermined path of the universe or the will of God expressed through natural order.</term>
For Remedies <term>Medelæ: Healing treatments or cures.</term> rise from a health-bringing spring,
And Medicines <term>Pharmaca: Drugs or medicinal preparations.</term> that restore dear lives to the wretched.
Now it is a manifest truth—by the laws of **Nature**, and by **Art**, <note>The "Art" refers to the Spagyric or Alchemical art, specifically the preparation of purified medicines.</note>
Not by chance—that human pains can be healed.
Henceforth, the untamed Chimeras shall submit their necks,
And the growing Hydras, being conquered, shall lay aside their rage,
Their insane furies, and their unmanageable venom, <note>The author uses mythological monsters like the Hydra and Chimera as metaphors for complex, recurring, or "venomous" diseases that were previously thought incurable.</note>
However much the hidden ghosts <note>original: "laruæ"; likely referring to the "masks" of disease—the deceptive symptoms that hide its true nature from the physician.</note> might conceal their tracks
And mock our slow senses with a wondrous veil.
Indeed, things previously confused by the broken law of Healing <term>Medicaminis: The art or substance of medicine.</term>
Are called back into a steady rank in a fortunate order.
No longer shall they torment sick souls with the pressure
Of countless fleets, or pour out hated potions.
A single Health <term>Salus: In this context, Salus refers to both bodily health and the concept of spiritual salvation.</term>, a single Sun illuminates the lands,
And alone drives the clouds from the overcast sky.
Thus, where the **Fates** wish, and the most sacred order of things,
All things change their turns, and the succeeding ages of the World
Once again set aside their accustomed laws.
Hail, auspicious day! Hail, long-awaited **Light**!
Have you come at last? With the circle of time completed,
Do you leave your secret chambers and your familiar bed?
You do not descend from the hall of some insignificant Divinity <term>Numinis: A divine power or presence.</term>,
Nor do you turn aside as a random guest to our shores:
You are driven by the commands of the Gods, and of the great Parent. <note>original: "magnique Parentis"; a reference to God as the creator and father of all.</note>

<meta>catchword: Auscul-</meta>

<summary>This page uses epic poetry to celebrate the shift from medical ignorance and "impure" theories to a new era of healing governed by the laws of Nature. It describes the triumph of the medical Art over monstrous, complex diseases, framing this scientific advancement as a divine gift or a long-awaited sunrise.</summary>
<keywords>Nature, Art, Alchemical Medicine, Healing, Hydra, Chimera, Divine Order, Enlightenment, Remedies</keywords>

--- Page 573 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from the previous discussion of the "Crossroads" of medical choice. It shifts from warning the reader about the "impure seeds" of false medicine to an epic exhortation. The poet addresses both the seeker and a "Leader"—likely a master physician or a personification of the Art itself—who is restoring the lost knowledge of Nature to the world.</meta>

You listen to these warnings—you, who now urge yourself to pass through these shadows, through places bristling with neglect and immersed in deep night, and who seek to gradually rekindle the extinguished **Light**. <note>The "Light" refers to the illumination of true medical or alchemical knowledge, which the author believes has been lost or obscured by time.</note> Proceed, child of the Gods, and glide with a gentle guidance where the decrees of the Higher Powers and their holy will call you.

You also, who gift us with this present favor, and come forward as a **Leader** <term>Dux: A guide or commander; here referring to the master who reveals the "Art."</term> on the high path, where no track of those who came before has yet turned onto the desired slope: 
You, who open the hidden entrances of **Nature**, who unlock her sacred halls and restore the honors of the lost **Art**: <note>The "Art" refers to the Spagyric or Alchemical art of medicine, which seeks to "restore" the purity of substances.</note>
You, who turn us toward the right-hand path—we who were wavering at the **Crossroads**, <note>original: "Biuio"; a reference to the "Choice of Hercules," a classic metaphor for choosing the difficult path of virtue over the easy path of vice or error.</note> and who have suffered a sad exile of journeys where Night, terror, and error torment those led astray:
Hail to your courage! Hail, most renowned with eternal praise, which neither devouring envy nor a long age shall extinguish.

Go, our glory, go! And draw blessed streams from the fertile fountain, and—as far as the sacred laws of veiled **Diana** <note>Diana, the goddess of the moon and the hunt, often represents the hidden or "silver" aspect of Nature in alchemical poetry. To "unveil" her is to reveal the secret workings of the natural world.</note> allow—sprinkle the herb that rises with difficulty among the bristling thorns and fierce thistles, and pour out long-lasting vital liquids. 
In this way, a joyful crop will flourish for you with full ears of grain, and the **Nymphs** will weave an unconquerable Crown for you from flowers.

O happy Souls, glowing with the love of Virtue, chosen race of great **Jupiter**, noble offspring, let us rise: a more favorable hour, accompanied by successful affairs, warns us not to slumber under this sky. Already, a flood of errors has submerged hearts surrounded by vast night in a hideous wave. 

Let us drive away the darkness, and let us venerate the Light we have attained. Relying on this Light, through a thousand tides, through a thousand **Charybdes**... <note>Charybdis: A mythical whirlpool from the Odyssey, used here to represent the extreme dangers or "swallowing" errors a physician might face.</note>

<summary>This page is a poetic exhortation calling for the restoration of the "Lost Art" of medicine and celebrating a "Leader" who guides seekers away from error and toward the "Light" of Nature. It uses classical imagery to frame medical discovery as a heroic, divinely-sanctioned quest.</summary>

<keywords>Light, The Art, Nature, Crossroads, Diana, virtue, medical guidance, poetic exhortation, Charybdis</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the epic exhortation from the previous page, moving from the praise of the "Leader" (the master physician) to a call to action. It frames the pursuit of medical and alchemical knowledge as a heroic journey into a "Kingdom of Virtue," guided by Mercury and protected by the Fates.</meta>

->*We shall penetrate the high walls of the blessed Kingdom.*<-
->*A difficult path must be attempted, but one which,*<-
->*once the hard labor is exhausted, will yield certain rewards.*<-
->*Let no force compel us to abandon this noble undertaking.*<-
->*Neither the furious rage of men, nor whatever unspeakable,*<-
->*heavy, sad, atrocious, or ruinous thing Erynnis hides,*<-
<note>original: "Erynnis"; In Greek mythology, the Erynnyes are the Furies, personifications of vengeance and divine wrath. Here, they represent the personified obstacles or malice that might hinder the seeker's progress.</note>
->*shall extinguish this light: for the Kingdom of Virtue flourishes*<-
->*and shall flourish eternally, as does the invincible will of the Gods.*<-
->*Therefore, with minds strengthened by unshaken vigor,*<-
->*let us pursue the majestic journey, and let us follow faithful*<-
->*Mercury, as he points out the Stars with his unerring wand.*<-
<term>Mercury: The messenger of the gods and patron of alchemy and medicine. His "wand" (the caduceus) was said to guide souls; here it guides the physician toward celestial or "spagyric" truths.</term>
->*The Fates will smooth the way; and if the shattered vault of heaven*<-
->*should fall, the ruins will strike us undaunted, though not with great weight.*<-
<note>This is a classical allusion to the Roman poet Horace, suggesting that the virtuous man remains fearless even if the world collapses around him.</note>

## JOHANNES PRATENSIS,
**a Dane and Doctor of Medicine, pays his votive offering of Ambrosia, as best he could, to the dawning Truth.**
<note>original: "Johannes Pratensis, Danus"; Pratensis (the Latinized form of the name Holm or Eng) was a prominent 16th-century Danish physician associated with the court and early chemical medicine. "Ambrosia" here refers to his poetic tribute.</note>

It is often interpreted as a reference to Jeremiah 23:29: "Is not my word like fire, declares the Lord, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?" It symbolizes the power of the printed word or the extraction of truth from hard matter.</note>
